-- The landing zone: telemetry packets exactly as the ground stations delivered them.
-- Three batches: batch 1 is 1 March 00:00-11:50, batch 2 is 1 March 12:00-23:50,
-- batch 3 is 2 March. One packet is one reading of one sensor, as JSON text.
CREATE TABLE landing_packet (
  batch_id    INTEGER NOT NULL,
  line_no     INTEGER NOT NULL,
  received_at TEXT    NOT NULL,
  body        TEXT,
  PRIMARY KEY (batch_id, line_no)
);
WITH RECURSIVE
  slot(s) AS (SELECT 0 UNION ALL SELECT s + 1 FROM slot WHERE s < 287),
  sat(n) AS (VALUES (1), (2), (3), (4), (5)),
  kind(k, code) AS (VALUES (1, 'batt_v'), (2, 'panel_t'), (3, 'cpu_t'), (4, 'wheel_rpm')),
  raw AS (
    SELECT s, n, k, code, (s + 2 * n) % 9 AS phase,
           CASE WHEN s < 72 THEN 1 WHEN s < 144 THEN 2 ELSE 3 END AS batch_id
    FROM slot, sat, kind
    WHERE NOT (n = 5 AND k = 4)
      AND NOT (n = 3 AND s BETWEEN 84 AND 95)
      AND NOT (n = 5 AND s BETWEEN 140 AND 147)
      AND NOT (n = 2 AND s BETWEEN 162 AND 165)
      AND NOT (n = 4 AND s = 200)
      AND NOT (n = 1 AND s BETWEEN 250 AND 251)
  ),
  valued AS (
    SELECT s, n, k, code, batch_id,
      CASE k
        WHEN 1 THEN round(
               (CASE WHEN phase < 6 THEN 28.0 + phase * 0.1 ELSE 27.6 - (phase - 6) * 0.4 END)
               - CASE WHEN n = 4 AND s BETWEEN 216 AND 233 THEN 1.5 ELSE 0 END
               - CASE WHEN n = 4 AND s BETWEEN 228 AND 233 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END, 2)
        WHEN 2 THEN CASE WHEN phase < 6 THEN 40 + phase * 5 ELSE -20 - (phase - 6) * 15 END
        WHEN 3 THEN CASE
               WHEN n = 2 AND s = 100 THEN 78.5
               WHEN n = 3 AND s BETWEEN 180 AND 185 THEN 60 + (s - 180) * 2.5
               ELSE 30 + ((s * 7 + n * 5) % 11) * 0.5 END
        ELSE 2000 + ((s * 13 + n * 17) % 21 - 10) * 15
      END AS v
    FROM raw
  )
INSERT INTO landing_packet (batch_id, line_no, received_at, body)
SELECT batch_id,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY batch_id ORDER BY s, n, k),
       CASE batch_id WHEN 1 THEN '2026-03-01 12:05:00' WHEN 2 THEN '2026-03-02 00:05:00' ELSE '2026-03-03 00:05:00' END,
       json_object('sat', 'ORB-' || n, 'sensor', code,
                   'ts', strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ', '2026-03-01', '+' || (s * 10) || ' minutes'),
                   'v', v)
FROM valued;

-- Batch 1: retransmits, and packets that must be quarantined.
INSERT INTO landing_packet (batch_id, line_no, received_at, body)
SELECT 1, (SELECT MAX(line_no) FROM landing_packet WHERE batch_id = 1) + ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY line_no), '2026-03-01 12:05:00', body
FROM landing_packet
WHERE batch_id = 1 AND body ->> '$.ts' = '2026-03-01T05:00:00Z' AND body ->> '$.sat' = 'ORB-1';
INSERT INTO landing_packet (batch_id, line_no, received_at, body) VALUES
  (1, 9001, '2026-03-01 12:05:00', '{"sat":"ORB-1","sensor":"batt_v","ts":"2026-03-01T05:10:00Z","v":28.1'),
  (1, 9002, '2026-03-01 12:05:00', '{"sat":"ORB-2","sensor":"cpu_t","ts":"2026-03-01T06:00:00Z"}'),
  (1, 9003, '2026-03-01 12:05:00', '{"sat":"ORB-1","sensor":"cpu_t","ts":"2026-03-01T25:10:00Z","v":31.0}'),
  (1, 9004, '2026-03-01 12:05:00', '{"sat":"ORB-3","sensor":"batt_v","ts":"2026-02-30T10:00:00Z","v":28.0}'),
  (1, 9005, '2026-03-01 12:05:00', '{"sat":"ORB-4","sensor":"panel_t","ts":"2026-03-01T07:00:00Z","v":"n/a"}'),
  (1, 9006, '2026-03-01 12:05:00', '{"sat":"ORB-9","sensor":"batt_v","ts":"2026-03-01T07:00:00Z","v":27.9}'),
  (1, 9007, '2026-03-01 12:05:00', '{"sat":"ORB-5","sensor":"wheel_rpm","ts":"2026-03-01T07:00:00Z","v":2010}'),
  (1, 9008, '2026-03-01 12:05:00', '{"sat":"ORB-2","sensor":"batt_v","ts":"2026-03-01T08:00:00Z","v":99.0}'),
  (1, 9009, '2026-03-01 12:05:00', '[1, 2, 3]'),
  (1, 9010, '2026-03-01 12:05:00', '{"sat":" orb-2 ","sensor":"Wheel_RPM","ts":"2026-03-01T11:55:00Z","v":1990}');

-- Batch 2: retransmits of batch 1, a correction, a changed mind inside the batch, and bad packets.
INSERT INTO landing_packet (batch_id, line_no, received_at, body)
SELECT 2, 9000 + ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY line_no), '2026-03-02 00:05:00', body
FROM landing_packet
WHERE batch_id = 1 AND line_no < 9000
  AND CASE WHEN json_valid(body) THEN body ->> '$.sat' = 'ORB-2'
           AND body ->> '$.ts' IN ('2026-03-01T11:40:00Z', '2026-03-01T11:50:00Z') END;
INSERT INTO landing_packet (batch_id, line_no, received_at, body) VALUES
  (2, 9101, '2026-03-02 00:05:00', '{"sat":"ORB-1","sensor":"batt_v","ts":"2026-03-01T10:50:00Z","v":28.35}'),
  (2, 9102, '2026-03-02 00:05:00', '{"sat":"ORB-3","sensor":"cpu_t","ts":"2026-03-01T18:20:00Z","v":44.0}'),
  (2, 9103, '2026-03-02 00:05:00', NULL),
  (2, 9104, '2026-03-02 00:05:00', '{"sensor":"cpu_t","ts":"2026-03-01T19:00:00Z","v":31.5}'),
  (2, 9105, '2026-03-02 00:05:00', '{"sat":"ORB-1","sensor":"panel_t","ts":"2026-03-01T19:00:00Z","v":400}'),
  (2, 9106, '2026-03-02 00:05:00', '{"sat":"ORB-3","sensor":"cpu_t","ts":"2026-03-01T18:20:00Z","v":33.0}');

-- Batch 3: late packets for 1 March, and bad packets.
INSERT INTO landing_packet (batch_id, line_no, received_at, body) VALUES
  (3, 9001, '2026-03-03 00:05:00', '{"sat":"ORB-5","sensor":"batt_v","ts":"2026-03-01T23:20:00Z","v":27.6}'),
  (3, 9002, '2026-03-03 00:05:00', '{"sat":"ORB-5","sensor":"panel_t","ts":"2026-03-01T23:20:00Z","v":-20}'),
  (3, 9003, '2026-03-03 00:05:00', '{"sat":"ORB-5","sensor":"cpu_t","ts":"2026-03-01T23:20:00Z","v":32.0}'),
  (3, 9004, '2026-03-03 00:05:00', '{"sat":"ORB-5","sensor":"batt_v","ts":"2026-03-01T23:30:00Z","v":27.2}'),
  (3, 9005, '2026-03-03 00:05:00', '{"sat":"ORB-5","sensor":"panel_t","ts":"2026-03-01T23:30:00Z","v":-35}'),
  (3, 9006, '2026-03-03 00:05:00', '{"sat":"ORB-5","sensor":"cpu_t","ts":"2026-03-01T23:30:00Z","v":30.0}'),
  (3, 9007, '2026-03-03 00:05:00', '{"sat":"ORB-4","sensor":"cpu_t","ts":"2026-03-02T10:00:00Z","v":-80}'),
  (3, 9008, '2026-03-03 00:05:00', '{"sat":"ORB-1","sensor":"cpu_t","ts":"2026/03/02 10:00:00","v":31.0}'),
  (3, 9009, '2026-03-03 00:05:00', '{"sat":"ORB-1","sensor":"rssi","ts":"2026-03-02T10:00:00Z","v":-92}'),
  (3, 9010, '2026-03-03 00:05:00', '{"sat":"ORB-4","sensor":"batt_v","ts":"2026-03-02T24:00:00Z","v":28.0}');
@end

=== cap-data-01 | Data system 1: the operational schema
--- teach
You have finished the SQL courses, from the first `SELECT` to query plans, and DSA I, where you met B-trees and indexes as ideas. This capstone puts all of it into one real system. Over 13 milestones you will build the **analytics warehouse** for ORBIT's fleet of satellites: the database that takes in raw telemetry, cleans it, stores it in a shape built for questions, keeps its numbers up to date as data arrives, and answers the operations team's questions fast. The finished project is over 2,000 lines of SQL.

### How the capstone works

Everything is one SQLite script. Each milestone's editor holds **the whole project so far**, with the new parts stubbed out and marked `TODO`. You fill them in. The checks run the whole script from an empty database every time, so they test the new milestone and re-run the key tests of the earlier ones. A change that breaks milestone 3 fails at milestone 9.

The only thing you are given is the **landing zone**: a table called `landing_packet`, where the ground stations drop telemetry exactly as it arrived. You will meet it in milestone 2. Everything else is yours.

Here is where the data will flow, one layer per group of milestones:

| layer | what it holds | milestones |
| --- | --- | --- |
| operational schema | the fleet as the operations team keeps it | 1 |
| staging | every packet that landed, parsed but not trusted | 2 |
| quarantine | packets that broke a rule, each with its reason | 3 |
| star schema | clean readings, shaped for questions | 4, 5 |
| rollups | hourly and daily summaries | 6 |
| reports | trends, outages, streaks, the morning report | 7, 8, 13 |
| tuning and safety | indexes, audit trail, data-quality checks | 9 to 12 |

### Milestone 1: the fleet

Before any telemetry can be trusted, the database has to know what exists: which satellites fly, which sensors each one carries, what values each kind of sensor can possibly report, and which ground stations listen when. That is the **operational schema**: the tables the operations team edits by hand. Every later layer checks incoming data against it.

The fleet has six satellites, `ORB-1` to `ORB-6` (ORB-6 is retired), four kinds of sensor (battery voltage, solar panel temperature, flight computer temperature and reaction wheel speed), four ground stations, and a schedule of 30 planned passes over two days.

### Design choice 1: one fact in one place

A **normalised** schema stores each fact about the world exactly once. The unit of battery voltage (`V`) is a fact about the *kind* of sensor, so it lives in `sensor_type`, once. It does not live on each of the five battery sensors.

The alternative is one wide table, with a row per sensor that repeats the satellite's name and status and the type's unit and limits. It is easy to query, and it is how a spreadsheet would do it. It is rejected because of the [[update anomaly|anomaly]]: when ORB-2 changes status, five rows must change together, and the day one of them is missed, the database disagrees with itself.

So there are five tables, and each one holds one kind of thing:

| table | one row is | key |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `satellite` | a satellite | `sat_id` |
| `sensor_type` | a kind of sensor, with its unit and limits | `type_code` |
| `sensor` | one sensor on one satellite | `sensor_id` |
| `ground_station` | a station | `station_id` |
| `contact_pass` | one planned pass of a satellite over a station | `pass_id` |

`sensor` is the link between the first two: it says which satellite carries which kind. Its two foreign keys point at them.

### Design choice 2: rules the database enforces

A rule written in application code holds only while every program that writes the table remembers it. A **constraint** is a rule the database itself checks on every insert and update, forever. For a system that other people and other programs will write to, the constraints *are* the specification. Every row that exists is a row that passed them. That is the table's **invariant**: a fact that is true of every row, always, because no statement can break it.

You know the four kinds from the advanced course. Here is what each one protects in this schema:

- `NOT NULL`: a satellite without a code, or a pass without a start time, means nothing.
- `UNIQUE`: two satellites called `ORB-3` would make every packet from ORB-3 ambiguous.
- `CHECK`: a value outside what can be true. A status that is not one of the three words. A pass that ends before it starts.
- `REFERENCES`: a sensor on a satellite that does not exist.

### Checks that test a value's shape

Some rules are about the *form* of a text. A satellite code looks like `ORB-` followed by digits. `GLOB`, SQLite's pattern match, says that exactly:

```sql
SELECT 'ORB-12' GLOB 'ORB-[0-9]*', 'orb-12' GLOB 'ORB-[0-9]*';
-- 1, 0
```

`[0-9]` is one digit and `*` is anything after it. Unlike `LIKE`, `GLOB` cares about capitals. It is a [[pattern, not a parser|glob-limits]], so `'ORB-1x'` also passes. Here that is fine; the goal is to stop obvious mistakes, like a code typed in small letters.

A date is harder. SQLite has no date type: dates are text. `date(x)` rewrites any date it understands as `YYYY-MM-DD`, and gives NULL for text it cannot read at all. So a **round trip** tests a date: rewrite it, and compare with the original.

```sql
SELECT '2024-02-29' IS date('2024-02-29'),
       '2025-02-29' IS date('2025-02-29'),
       '2025-2-3'   IS date('2025-2-3'),
       '2025-2-3'   =  date('2025-2-3');
-- 1, 0, 0, NULL
```

2024 was a leap year, so 29 February is real. In 2025 it is not, and SQLite quietly [[rolls it over to 1 March|rollover]], so the round trip fails. `'2025-2-3'` is not a shape `date()` reads at all, so it gives NULL.

Look at the last two columns. With `=`, comparing anything with NULL gives NULL, and a `CHECK` whose test comes out NULL **passes**. So `CHECK (d = date(d))` would let `'2025-2-3'` in. `IS` compares the way you mean: it treats NULL as a value, so `'2025-2-3' IS NULL` is plain false and the check fails, as it should. Write date checks with `IS`.

The same trick with `datetime()` tests a full `'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'`, with one more quirk. Without a modifier, `datetime()` copies a time like `24:30:00` through untouched, so it would pass. A modifier that changes nothing, `'+0 seconds'`, makes SQLite do the date arithmetic, which turns 24:30 into 00:30 the next day, so the round trip fails as it should: `aos IS datetime(aos, '+0 seconds')`.

Dates in this form have one more gift: they sort as text in time order. So `CHECK (status_since >= launched_on)` compares two dates correctly with a plain `>=`.

### Two SQLite traps

Two of SQLite's defaults are wrong for a system like this one, and both fail silently.

1. **Foreign keys are off.** SQLite checks `REFERENCES` only after `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;`, and the setting belongs to the [[connection|connection]], not the file. The script turns it on in its first line.
2. **A `TEXT PRIMARY KEY` accepts NULL.** For historical reasons, only an `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` refuses NULL by itself. Write `type_code TEXT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY`.

### Two views that later layers lean on

A **view** is a saved query. Two views finish this milestone.

`v_sensor_catalog` joins the three fleet tables into one row per sensor: its id, its satellite's id, code and status, its type, unit and limits. In milestone 3, every incoming packet names a satellite code and a sensor type, and this view is the one place that turns that pair into a sensor. Keeping that lookup in one view means there is one place to fix it.

`v_fleet_roster` is the morning roster: one row per satellite, with how many sensors it carries, their type codes joined with commas in alphabetical order, and how many passes are planned for it. A satellite with no sensors must still appear, with 0 and an empty text. That needs a `LEFT JOIN`, and `COUNT(se.sensor_id)` rather than `COUNT(*)`: `COUNT(*)` counts the one row the `LEFT JOIN` makes for a satellite with no match, and would say 1.

`group_concat(x, ',')` joins the texts of a group, in the order the rows reach it. After a join and a `GROUP BY`, that order is the database's choice, not yours: here it follows the sensor ids, so ORB-1's list would come out `batt_v,panel_t,cpu_t,…`. To choose the order, build each satellite's list in a subquery of its own that sorts first. The shape, for some other list:

```sql fragment
(SELECT group_concat(name, ';') FROM (SELECT name FROM crew WHERE ship_id = s.ship_id ORDER BY name))
```

### How to test it: known answers

Every milestone ends with a **known-answer test**. You work out the right numbers by hand, from the data, and store them in a table. A test view compares them with what the database says and returns the rows that disagree. An empty result is a pass.

The expectations live in one table for all simple counts, `expect_count (test, item, expected)`. For this milestone the hand counts are the roster's: how many sensors and passes each satellite has. `test_roster` returns every `(test, item)` where the expected count and the actual count differ, in either direction. A missing satellite counts as a difference too, so it needs a `FULL OUTER JOIN`, which keeps the unmatched rows of both sides:

```sql fragment
FROM (SELECT test, item, expected FROM expect_count WHERE ...) e
FULL OUTER JOIN (...actual counts...) a ON a.test = e.test AND a.item = e.item
WHERE e.expected IS NOT a.actual
```

`IS NOT` is `<>` that treats NULL as a value: `3 IS NOT NULL` is true, where `3 <> NULL` is NULL and would hide the missing row. Finally `test_summary` (given) counts the failing rows of every test. From now on, a green build is `test_summary` showing zeros.

A test that passes proves little until you have seen it fail. So the checks also break something on purpose, inside a [[savepoint|savepoint]], and make sure your test notices.

### What it costs

A `CHECK` or `NOT NULL` costs a few comparisons per row written: O(1). `UNIQUE` and `PRIMARY KEY` are kept in a **B-tree index**, the balanced search tree from DSA I, so checking a new key costs O(log n). SQLite builds those indexes for you; you will see their names, `sqlite_autoindex_…`, in query plans in milestone 9. A foreign key looks the parent key up in the parent's primary key index: O(log n) too. The fleet tables are tiny, so none of this matters here. It matters a great deal for the fact table in milestone 4, which gains a row every few seconds.

### Where this is used

Every real operations system has a layer like this: the equipment list, the configuration, the plan. Mission control software keeps the spacecraft and ground station catalogues as data exactly so that a new satellite is a new row, not a new release.

**Watch out:** it is easy to test constraints by only inserting good data. Every constraint here is tested the other way: by trying a row that breaks it and checking that it was refused. With `INSERT OR IGNORE`, a refused row is skipped quietly, so you can count what got in. One exception: a foreign key violation is never ignored, it always stops the script. And if `PRAGMA foreign_keys` is off, it is never even checked.

::: context anomaly What an update anomaly is
An **update anomaly** is what happens when one fact is stored in several places and a change reaches only some of them. If each sensor row repeated its satellite's status, marking ORB-2 as in safe mode would mean updating four rows. Miss one, and a report that counts sensors in safe mode gets a different answer from one that counts satellites. Normalising removes the chance: the status is stored once, and every query reads the same copy. The cost is joins at query time, which is exactly the cost the star schema in milestone 4 will choose to pay back the other way, for speed.
:::

::: context glob-limits What GLOB can and cannot say
`GLOB` patterns have three special marks: `*` is any run of characters, `?` is one character, and `[...]` is one character from a set, like `[0-9]`. That is enough to say "starts with ORB- and a digit", but not "only digits after the dash", because there is no way to repeat a set. For that you would need a regular expression, which SQLite does not include by default. In practice, shape checks aim at the mistakes people really make, like typing codes in small letters or with a space, rather than proving a value perfect.
:::

::: context rollover Why SQLite rolls dates over
SQLite's date functions accept a day number up to 31 in every month and then do the arithmetic, so `date('2025-02-30')` is `'2025-03-02'`: two days after 28 February. That is handy for date arithmetic and dangerous for validation, because a typo becomes a different, real date with no error. The round trip catches it: the rewritten date is not the text you started with. You will meet the same trap in milestone 3, where a packet arrives stamped 30 February.
:::

::: context connection A connection and its settings
A **connection** is one program's open line to the database file. Each connection has its own settings, and `PRAGMA foreign_keys` is one of them. A second program that opens the same file starts with foreign keys off again, and can insert rows that break every `REFERENCES` in the schema. That is why this script turns the pragma on in its very first statement, and why real SQLite applications set it every time they connect.
:::

::: context savepoint Trying something and taking it back
`SAVEPOINT name` marks a point in time, `ROLLBACK TO name` undoes everything since that mark, and `RELEASE name` forgets the mark. It works like `BEGIN` and `ROLLBACK`, but savepoints can be nested. The checks use one to break the data on purpose, for example by deleting a sensor, run your test view, and then roll back, so the next check starts from the real data again.
:::
--- task
Build the operational schema. The reference data (the `INSERT` statements) is already in the starter; your tables must accept every row of it.

1. Make `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;` the first statement.
2. Give the five tables these rules, keeping the column names and order:
   - `satellite`: `code` required, unique, and matching `GLOB 'ORB-[0-9]*'`; `name` required; `launched_on` required and a real date (`launched_on IS date(launched_on)`); `status` required, default `'active'`, one of `'active'`, `'safe_mode'`, `'retired'`; `status_since` required and not before `launched_on`.
   - `sensor_type`: `type_code` a primary key that is never NULL and equal to `lower(type_code)`; every other column required; `min_valid < max_valid`.
   - `sensor`: `sat_id` required and referencing `satellite (sat_id)`; `type_code` required and referencing `sensor_type (type_code)`; each `(sat_id, type_code)` pair unique.
   - `ground_station`: `code` required, unique, three characters long and all capitals (`code = upper(code)`); `name` required; `latitude` required, between -90 and 90; `longitude` required, between -180 and 180.
   - `contact_pass`: `sat_id` required, referencing `satellite`; `station_id` required, referencing `ground_station`; `aos` and `los` required, and each a real moment in the standard form (`aos IS datetime(aos, '+0 seconds')`, and the same for `los`); `los > aos`; each `(sat_id, aos)` pair unique.
3. Create the view `v_sensor_catalog` with the columns `sensor_id`, `sat_id`, `sat_code` (the satellite's `code`), `sat_status`, `type_code`, `unit`, `min_valid`, `max_valid`: one row per sensor.
4. Create the view `v_fleet_roster` with the columns `sat_code`, `name`, `status`, `sensors` (how many sensors it carries), `sensor_types` (their type codes in alphabetical order joined with `','`, or `''` when it has none) and `passes` (how many rows of `contact_pass` it has). One row per satellite, including one with no sensors, ordered by `sat_code`.
5. Add the known-answer test. Insert these rows into `expect_count`: test `'sensors'` with items `'ORB-1'` to `'ORB-6'` and counts 4, 4, 4, 4, 3, 4; test `'passes'` with the same items and counts 6, 6, 6, 6, 6, 0. Then replace the stub `test_roster` with a view of the columns `test`, `item`, `expected`, `actual` that returns one row for every `(test, item)` where the count in `expect_count` and the count in `v_fleet_roster` differ, including an item missing from either side. `test_summary` is given.
--- starter
-- =====================================================================
--  ORBIT fleet telemetry warehouse
--  Milestone 1: the operational schema. Replace every TODO.
-- =====================================================================

-- TODO: turn on foreign keys for this connection.

CREATE TABLE satellite (
  sat_id       INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  code         TEXT,     -- TODO: required, unique, shaped like ORB-7
  name         TEXT,     -- TODO: required
  launched_on  TEXT,     -- TODO: required, a real YYYY-MM-DD date
  status       TEXT,     -- TODO: required, default 'active', one of three words
  status_since TEXT      -- TODO: required, not before launched_on
);

CREATE TABLE sensor_type (
  type_code  TEXT PRIMARY KEY,   -- TODO: never NULL, always lower case
  label      TEXT,
  unit       TEXT,
  min_valid  REAL,
  max_valid  REAL
  -- TODO: min_valid must be below max_valid
);

CREATE TABLE sensor (
  sensor_id  INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  sat_id     INTEGER,   -- TODO: required, points at satellite
  type_code  TEXT       -- TODO: required, points at sensor_type
  -- TODO: a satellite carries at most one sensor of each type
);

CREATE TABLE ground_station (
  station_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  code       TEXT,   -- TODO: required, unique, three capital letters
  name       TEXT,
  latitude   REAL,   -- TODO: -90 to 90
  longitude  REAL    -- TODO: -180 to 180
);

CREATE TABLE contact_pass (
  pass_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  sat_id     INTEGER,   -- TODO: required, points at satellite
  station_id INTEGER,   -- TODO: required, points at ground_station
  aos        TEXT,      -- TODO: required, a real 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'
  los        TEXT       -- TODO: required, a real 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS', after aos
  -- TODO: a satellite cannot start two passes at the same moment
);

-- Reference data. Sensor ids are the satellite number times ten plus a
-- channel, so 23 is ORB-2's flight computer thermometer.
INSERT INTO satellite (sat_id, code, name, launched_on, status, status_since) VALUES
  (1, 'ORB-1', 'Kestrel', '2021-04-12', 'active',  '2021-04-12'),
  (2, 'ORB-2', 'Heron',   '2021-04-12', 'active',  '2021-04-12'),
  (3, 'ORB-3', 'Osprey',  '2022-09-30', 'active',  '2022-09-30'),

--- solution
-- =====================================================================
--  ORBIT fleet telemetry warehouse
--
--  One script builds the whole database from an empty file that holds
--  only the landing zone (landing_packet). The layers, in the order the
--  data flows through them:
--
--    1. operational schema   the fleet, as the operations team keeps it
--    2. pipeline control     runs and steps, one trigger per step
--    3. staging              every landed packet, parsed, not trusted
--    4. quarantine           rejected packets, each with one reason
--    5. star schema          dimensions and the fact table
--    6. rollups              hourly and daily aggregates
--    7. trend reports        window functions over the facts
--    8. gaps and islands     outages, empty hours, low-battery streaks
--    9. data quality         checks that must return zero rows
--   10. report suite         what operations reads every morning
--
--  Conventions: times are UTC text 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'; every step can
--  be rerun for the same batch without changing the result.
-- =====================================================================

PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 1. Operational schema: the fleet as the operations team keeps it.
--    Normalised: each fact about the fleet is stored exactly once, and
--    the constraints refuse any row that could not be true.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE satellite (
  sat_id       INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  code         TEXT    NOT NULL UNIQUE CHECK (code GLOB 'ORB-[0-9]*'),
  name         TEXT    NOT NULL,
  launched_on  TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (launched_on IS date(launched_on)),
  status       TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active'
                       CHECK (status IN ('active', 'safe_mode', 'retired')),
  status_since TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (status_since >= launched_on)
);

CREATE TABLE sensor_type (
  type_code  TEXT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY CHECK (type_code = lower(type_code)),
  label      TEXT NOT NULL,
  unit       TEXT NOT NULL,
  min_valid  REAL NOT NULL,
  max_valid  REAL NOT NULL,
  CHECK (min_valid < max_valid)
);

CREATE TABLE sensor (
  sensor_id  INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  sat_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES satellite (sat_id),
  type_code  TEXT    NOT NULL REFERENCES sensor_type (type_code),
  UNIQUE (sat_id, type_code)
);

CREATE TABLE ground_station (
  station_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  code       TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE CHECK (length(code) = 3 AND code = upper(code)),
  name       TEXT NOT NULL,
  latitude   REAL NOT NULL CHECK (latitude BETWEEN -90 AND 90),
  longitude  REAL NOT NULL CHECK (longitude BETWEEN -180 AND 180)
);

-- A planned contact: the satellite is above the station's horizon from
-- aos (acquisition of signal) until los (loss of signal).
CREATE TABLE contact_pass (
  pass_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  sat_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES satellite (sat_id),
  station_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES ground_station (station_id),
  aos        TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (aos IS datetime(aos, '+0 seconds')),
  los        TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (los IS datetime(los, '+0 seconds')),
  CHECK (los > aos),
  UNIQUE (sat_id, aos)
);

-- The one place that turns packet codes into a sensor: which satellite
-- carries which kind of sensor, with the limits that make a value possible.
CREATE VIEW v_sensor_catalog AS
SELECT se.sensor_id,
       sa.sat_id,
       sa.code   AS sat_code,
       sa.status AS sat_status,
       st.type_code,
       st.unit,
       st.min_valid,
       st.max_valid
FROM sensor se
JOIN satellite   sa ON sa.sat_id    = se.sat_id
JOIN sensor_type st ON st.type_code = se.type_code;

-- The roster the operations team reads every morning.
CREATE VIEW v_fleet_roster AS
SELECT sa.code AS sat_code,
       sa.name,
       sa.status,
       COUNT(se.sensor_id) AS sensors,
       COALESCE((SELECT group_concat(type_code, ',')
                 FROM (SELECT type_code FROM sensor
                       WHERE sat_id = sa.sat_id
                       ORDER BY type_code)), '') AS sensor_types,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM contact_pass p WHERE p.sat_id = sa.sat_id) AS passes
FROM satellite sa
LEFT JOIN sensor se ON se.sat_id = sa.sat_id
GROUP BY sa.sat_id
ORDER BY sa.code;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 12. Known-answer tests. Each expected value below was worked out by
--     hand from the development window's packets, not copied from the
--     pipeline's output. Each test_ view returns the rows where the
--     warehouse disagrees with the hand count: empty means pass.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE expect_count (
  test     TEXT    NOT NULL,
  item     TEXT    NOT NULL,
  expected INTEGER NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (test, item)
);

INSERT INTO expect_count (test, item, expected) VALUES
  ('sensors', 'ORB-1', 4), ('sensors', 'ORB-2', 4), ('sensors', 'ORB-3', 4),
  ('sensors', 'ORB-4', 4), ('sensors', 'ORB-5', 3), ('sensors', 'ORB-6', 4),
  ('passes',  'ORB-1', 6), ('passes',  'ORB-2', 6), ('passes',  'ORB-3', 6),
  ('passes',  'ORB-4', 6), ('passes',  'ORB-5', 6), ('passes',  'ORB-6', 0);

CREATE VIEW test_roster AS
SELECT COALESCE(e.test, a.test) AS test,
       COALESCE(e.item, a.item) AS item,
       e.expected,
       a.actual
FROM (SELECT test, item, expected FROM expect_count
      WHERE test IN ('sensors', 'passes')) e
FULL OUTER JOIN (SELECT 'sensors' AS test, sat_code AS item, sensors AS actual FROM v_fleet_roster
                 UNION ALL
                 SELECT 'passes', sat_code, passes FROM v_fleet_roster) a
  ON a.test = e.test AND a.item = e.item
WHERE e.expected IS NOT a.actual;

-- One line per test: how many rows disagree. All zeros is a green build.
CREATE VIEW test_summary AS
SELECT test, failures FROM (
            SELECT 'roster'      AS test, COUNT(*) AS failures FROM test_roster
);
--- hint
Work table by table, and put each rule where it belongs: a rule about one column goes on that column, and a rule about two columns (`min_valid < max_valid`, `los > aos`, the unique pairs) goes at the end of the table as its own line. Remember that `TEXT PRIMARY KEY` alone lets NULL in.
--- hint
For the roster, start from `satellite`, `LEFT JOIN sensor`, group by the satellite, and count `se.sensor_id`, not `*`. The sorted list and the passes count are easiest as subqueries in the `SELECT` list; wrap the list in `COALESCE(…, '')`.
--- hint
`test_roster` needs the actual counts in the same shape as `expect_count`: `SELECT 'sensors' AS test, sat_code AS item, sensors AS actual FROM v_fleet_roster UNION ALL SELECT 'passes', sat_code, passes FROM v_fleet_roster`. `FULL OUTER JOIN` it with the expected rows on `test` and `item`, and keep the rows where `e.expected IS NOT a.actual`.

+++ practice | Battery packs with rules
--- schema
-- This problem starts from an empty database.
--- task
The spares store keeps one row per battery pack. Create the table `battery_pack` with these columns and rules:

- `pack_id`: `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`
- `serial`: required and unique text
- `chemistry`: required, one of `'li-ion'`, `'nimh'`, `'lifepo4'`
- `capacity_wh`: required number, greater than 0
- `cycles`: required whole number, default 0, never negative

The checks try good and bad rows with `INSERT OR IGNORE`, so a row that breaks a rule must be refused, not stored.
--- starter
CREATE TABLE battery_pack (
  pack_id     INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  serial      TEXT,
  chemistry   TEXT,
  capacity_wh REAL,
  cycles      INTEGER
);
--- solution
CREATE TABLE battery_pack (
  pack_id     INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  serial      TEXT    NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  chemistry   TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (chemistry IN ('li-ion', 'nimh', 'lifepo4')),
  capacity_wh REAL    NOT NULL CHECK (capacity_wh > 0),
  cycles      INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (cycles >= 0)
);
--- hint
Each rule belongs to one column, so write it on that column's line: `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`, `DEFAULT 0` and a `CHECK (...)`.
--- hint
The chemistry rule is `CHECK (chemistry IN ('li-ion', 'nimh', 'lifepo4'))`. "Greater than 0" and "never negative" are different tests: `> 0` and `>= 0`.
--- check query | Good packs go in, and cycles defaults to 0

=> [[1, 0], [2, 12]]
--- check query | A repeated serial and an unknown chemistry are refused

=> [[2]]

INSERT OR IGNORE INTO battery_pack (pack_id, serial, chemistry, capacity_wh, cycles) VALUES (6, 'BP-006', 'nimh', 40, -1);
INSERT OR IGNORE INTO battery_pack (pack_id, serial, chemistry, capacity_wh) VALUES (7, NULL, 'nimh', 40);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM battery_pack
=> [[2]]
--- check query | A pack with zero cycles is fine

+++ practice | Crew assignments: one seat per role
--- schema
-- This problem starts from an empty database.
--- task
Create three tables for crew assignments, and turn on foreign keys first with `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;`.

- `astronaut (astro_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)`
- `mission (mission_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, code TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE)`
- `assignment`, with the columns `astro_id`, `mission_id` and `role`:
  - `astro_id` is required and references `astronaut (astro_id)`;
  - `mission_id` is required and references `mission (mission_id)`;
  - `role` is required and one of `'commander'`, `'pilot'`, `'specialist'`;
  - an astronaut holds at most one role on each mission;
  - each role on a mission is held by at most one astronaut.

The last two rules are each about two columns together.
--- starter
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;

CREATE TABLE astronaut (astro_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE mission (mission_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, code TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE);

CREATE TABLE assignment (
  astro_id   INTEGER,
  mission_id INTEGER,
  role       TEXT
);
--- solution
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;

CREATE TABLE astronaut (astro_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE mission (mission_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, code TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE);

CREATE TABLE assignment (
  astro_id   INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES astronaut (astro_id),
  mission_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES mission (mission_id),
  role       TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (role IN ('commander', 'pilot', 'specialist')),
  UNIQUE (astro_id, mission_id),
  UNIQUE (mission_id, role)
);
--- hint
"At most one role per astronaut per mission" means the pair `(astro_id, mission_id)` never repeats. Say it as a line of its own at the end of the table.
--- hint
The seat rule is the same idea with a different pair: `(mission_id, role)` never repeats. A table can have as many `UNIQUE (...)` lines as it needs.
--- check query | The foreign keys are declared
SELECT "table", "from" FROM pragma_foreign_key_list('assignment') ORDER BY "from"
=> [["astronaut", "astro_id"], ["mission", "mission_id"]]

=> [[5]]
--- check query | A second role for the same person on one mission is refused

=> [[1]]
--- check query | A second commander on M-10 is refused, but Di can still fly as M-11's specialist

=> [[10, "commander", 1], [11, "commander", 2], [11, "specialist", 4]]
--- check query | An unknown role and a missing mission are refused

=> [[1]]

+++ practice | Antennas per station, zero included
--- schema
CREATE TABLE station (station_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, code TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE);
CREATE TABLE antenna (
  antenna_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  station_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES station (station_id),
  band       TEXT NOT NULL,
  dish_m     REAL NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO station VALUES (1, 'SVB'), (2, 'AWA'), (3, 'PUN'), (4, 'KIR');
INSERT INTO antenna VALUES
  (1, 1, 'X', 13.0), (2, 1, 'S', 7.3), (3, 1, 'X', 11.0),
  (4, 2, 'S', 9.0),
  (5, 3, 'Ka', 13.5), (6, 3, 'X', 13.5);
--- task
Each ground station in `station (station_id, code)` has antennas in `antenna (antenna_id, station_id, band, dish_m)`. Station `KIR` has none yet.

Create the view `station_summary` with one row per station and these columns:

- `code`
- `antennas`: how many antennas it has (0 for none)
- `bands`: its distinct bands in alphabetical order joined with `'/'`, or `''` when it has none (SVB's is `'S/X'`)
- `largest_m`: its largest dish, or NULL when it has none

Order the view by `code`.
--- starter
CREATE VIEW station_summary AS
SELECT s.code,
       COUNT(*) AS antennas,
       group_concat(a.band, '/') AS bands,
       MAX(a.dish_m) AS largest_m
FROM station s
JOIN antenna a ON a.station_id = s.station_id
GROUP BY s.station_id
ORDER BY s.code;
--- solution
CREATE VIEW station_summary AS
SELECT s.code,
       COUNT(a.antenna_id) AS antennas,
       COALESCE((SELECT group_concat(band, '/')
                 FROM (SELECT DISTINCT band FROM antenna
                       WHERE station_id = s.station_id ORDER BY band)), '') AS bands,
       MAX(a.dish_m) AS largest_m
FROM station s
LEFT JOIN antenna a ON a.station_id = s.station_id
GROUP BY s.station_id
ORDER BY s.code;
--- hint
KIR vanishes because of the inner `JOIN`. With a `LEFT JOIN` it comes back, and then `COUNT(*)` says 1 for it: count a column of the antenna instead.
--- hint
The bands need three things: distinct, sorted, joined. A subquery per station can do all three: `SELECT group_concat(band, '/') FROM (SELECT DISTINCT band FROM antenna WHERE station_id = s.station_id ORDER BY band)`. Wrap it in `COALESCE(…, '')`.
--- check query | Four rows, in order, with KIR at 0
SELECT * FROM station_summary
=> [["AWA", 1, "S", 9.0], ["KIR", 0, "", null], ["PUN", 2, "Ka/X", 13.5], ["SVB", 3, "S/X", 13.0]]
--- check query | SVB lists X once
SELECT bands FROM station_summary WHERE code = 'SVB'
=> [["S/X"]]
--- check query | A new station with no antennas appears too
INSERT INTO station VALUES (5, 'ALB');
SELECT code, antennas, bands, largest_m FROM station_summary WHERE code = 'ALB'
=> [["ALB", 0, "", null]]

+++ practice | Real dates only
--- schema
-- This problem starts from an empty database.
--- task
Create the table `maintenance` with the columns `job_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`, `done_on TEXT` and `done_at TEXT`:

- `done_on` is required and must be a real date written exactly as `YYYY-MM-DD`.
- `done_at` may be NULL. When it is present, it must be a real moment written exactly as `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS`, on the same day as `done_on`.

Use round trips with `date()` and `datetime()`. The checks try dates that do not exist, dates in other shapes, and the leap day of 2024.
--- starter
CREATE TABLE maintenance (
  job_id  INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  done_on TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (done_on = date(done_on)),
  done_at TEXT
);
--- solution
CREATE TABLE maintenance (
  job_id  INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  done_on TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (done_on IS date(done_on)),
  done_at TEXT CHECK (done_at IS NULL
                      OR (done_at IS datetime(done_at) AND date(done_at) = done_on))
);
--- hint
The starter's `done_on = date(done_on)` lets `'2026-3-1'` in. `date('2026-3-1')` is NULL, the comparison is NULL, and a `CHECK` that works out to NULL passes. Which comparison treats NULL as an ordinary value?
--- hint
`done_on IS date(done_on)` is false for a shape `date()` cannot read. For `done_at`, allow NULL first, then test the round trip with `datetime()` and the day: `done_at IS NULL OR (done_at IS datetime(done_at) AND date(done_at) = done_on)`.
--- check query | Real dates go in, including 29 February 2024
INSERT OR IGNORE INTO maintenance VALUES (1, '2024-02-29', NULL), (2, '2026-03-01', '2026-03-01 07:30:00');
SELECT job_id FROM maintenance ORDER BY job_id
=> [[1], [2]]
--- check query | Dates that do not exist are refused
INSERT OR IGNORE INTO maintenance VALUES (3, '2025-02-29', NULL), (4, '2026-04-31', NULL), (5, '2026-13-01', NULL);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM maintenance
=> [[2]]
--- check query | Other shapes are refused
INSERT OR IGNORE INTO maintenance VALUES (6, '2026-3-1', NULL), (7, '01/03/2026', NULL), (8, '2026-03-01 00:00:00', NULL);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM maintenance
=> [[2]]
--- check query | done_at must be a real moment, in the standard shape, on the same day
INSERT OR IGNORE INTO maintenance VALUES (9, '2026-03-02', '2026-03-03 01:00:00'), (10, '2026-03-02', '2026-03-02T01:00:00'), (11, '2026-03-02', '2026-03-02 25:00:00'), (12, '2026-03-02', '2026-03-02 23:59:59');
SELECT group_concat(job_id) FROM maintenance WHERE job_id > 8
=> [["12"]]

+++ practice | The key that let NULL in
--- schema
-- This problem starts from an empty database.
--- task
This schema was meant to refuse a component type without a code, and a component whose type does not exist. It does neither: a type with a NULL code goes in, and nothing ever checks the `REFERENCES`.

```sql
CREATE TABLE component_type (
  code  TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  label TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE component (
  component_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  type_code    TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES component_type (code)
);
```

Fix it so that `component_type` refuses a NULL code and the foreign key is enforced. Keep both tables' columns as they are.
--- starter
CREATE TABLE component_type (
  code  TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  label TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE component (
  component_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  type_code    TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES component_type (code)
);
--- solution
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;

CREATE TABLE component_type (
  code  TEXT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
  label TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE component (
  component_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  type_code    TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES component_type (code)
);
--- hint
Two separate SQLite defaults are at work. One is about which primary keys refuse NULL on their own. The other is about whether `REFERENCES` is checked at all.
--- hint
Only an `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` refuses NULL by itself, so add `NOT NULL` to `code`. Foreign keys are enforced only after `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;`, which must come before any insert.
--- check query | Foreign keys are enforced
SELECT foreign_keys FROM pragma_foreign_keys
=> [[1]]
--- check query | A type with a NULL code is refused, a real one goes in
INSERT OR IGNORE INTO component_type VALUES (NULL, 'Mystery');
INSERT OR IGNORE INTO component_type VALUES ('valve', 'Valve');
SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(code IS NULL) FROM component_type
=> [[1, 0]]
--- check query | A component of a real type goes in

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM component
=> [[1]]
--- check query | The foreign key still points at component_type
SELECT "table", "from", "to" FROM pragma_foreign_key_list('component')
=> [["component_type", "type_code", "code"]]

+++ practice | From one flat sheet to three tables
--- schema
CREATE TABLE flat_config (
  sat_code  TEXT,
  sat_name  TEXT,
  type_code TEXT,
  unit      TEXT,
  min_valid REAL,
  max_valid REAL
);
INSERT INTO flat_config VALUES
  ('LYR-1', 'Lyra A', 'batt_v', 'V', 20, 34),
  ('LYR-1', 'Lyra A', 'mag_x', 'nT', -60000, 60000),
  ('LYR-2', 'Lyra B', 'batt_v', 'V', 20, 34),
  ('LYR-2', 'Lyra B', 'mag_x', 'nT', -60000, 60000),
  ('LYR-2', 'Lyra B', 'sun_deg', 'deg', 0, 180),
  ('LYR-3', 'Lyra C', 'batt_v', 'V', 20, 34);
--- task
A mission's configuration arrived as one flat sheet, `flat_config (sat_code, sat_name, type_code, unit, min_valid, max_valid)`, one row per sensor, with the satellite's name and the type's unit and limits repeated on every row.

Normalise it:

1. Create `sat (sat_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, code TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, name TEXT NOT NULL)`.
2. Create `kind (type_code TEXT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY, unit TEXT NOT NULL, min_valid REAL NOT NULL, max_valid REAL NOT NULL)`.
3. Create `fitted (sat_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES sat (sat_id), type_code TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES kind (type_code), PRIMARY KEY (sat_id, type_code))`.
4. Fill all three from `flat_config` with `INSERT … SELECT`. Number the satellites 1, 2, 3 in order of code.
5. Create the view `flat_again` that joins them back into the six original rows, with the same six column names as `flat_config`.
--- starter
CREATE TABLE sat (sat_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, code TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, name TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE kind (type_code TEXT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY, unit TEXT NOT NULL, min_valid REAL NOT NULL, max_valid REAL NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE fitted (
  sat_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES sat (sat_id),
  type_code TEXT    NOT NULL REFERENCES kind (type_code),
  PRIMARY KEY (sat_id, type_code)
);
--- solution
CREATE TABLE sat (sat_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, code TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, name TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE kind (type_code TEXT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY, unit TEXT NOT NULL, min_valid REAL NOT NULL, max_valid REAL NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE fitted (
  sat_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES sat (sat_id),
  type_code TEXT    NOT NULL REFERENCES kind (type_code),
  PRIMARY KEY (sat_id, type_code)
);

INSERT INTO sat (code, name)
SELECT DISTINCT sat_code, sat_name FROM flat_config ORDER BY sat_code;

INSERT INTO kind (type_code, unit, min_valid, max_valid)
SELECT DISTINCT type_code, unit, min_valid, max_valid FROM flat_config;

INSERT INTO fitted (sat_id, type_code)
SELECT s.sat_id, f.type_code
FROM flat_config f
JOIN sat s ON s.code = f.sat_code;

CREATE VIEW flat_again AS
SELECT s.code AS sat_code, s.name AS sat_name, k.type_code, k.unit, k.min_valid, k.max_valid
FROM fitted x
JOIN sat  s ON s.sat_id = x.sat_id
JOIN kind k ON k.type_code = x.type_code;
--- hint
Fill the parents first: `sat` and `kind` each get one row per distinct satellite or type, with `SELECT DISTINCT`. Leave out `sat_id` in the insert, and the `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` numbers the rows in the order they arrive.
--- hint
`fitted` needs the new `sat_id` for each flat row: join `flat_config` to `sat` on the code. The view joins the three tables back together and renames the columns to the flat names.
--- check query | 3 satellites, 3 kinds, 6 fittings
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sat), (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM kind), (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM fitted)
=> [[3, 3, 6]]
--- check query | The satellites are numbered in order of code
SELECT sat_id, code, name FROM sat ORDER BY sat_id
=> [[1, "LYR-1", "Lyra A"], [2, "LYR-2", "Lyra B"], [3, "LYR-3", "Lyra C"]]
--- check query | flat_again gives back exactly the original rows
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT * FROM flat_again EXCEPT SELECT * FROM flat_config)
=> [[0]]
--- check query | …and none are lost
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT * FROM flat_config EXCEPT SELECT * FROM flat_again)
=> [[0]]
--- check query | The unit of mag_x is stored once
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM kind WHERE type_code = 'mag_x'
=> [[1]]

=== cap-data-02 | Data system 2: landing and staging packets
--- teach
Last milestone you built the fleet: the tables that say what exists. Now telemetry arrives. This milestone takes every packet the ground stations delivered into the warehouse's first layer, **staging**, and builds the machinery that runs the pipeline one batch at a time.

### The landing zone

The ground stations drop what they receive into `landing_packet`, one row per packet, and never change it afterwards. It is the one table you are given:

| column | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `batch_id` | the delivery it came in: 1, 2 or 3 |
| `line_no` | its line within the delivery |
| `received_at` | when the delivery reached the ground |
| `body` | the packet, as JSON text |

Batch 1 holds 1 March from midnight to noon, batch 2 the rest of 1 March, and batch 3 all of 2 March: 5,410 packets in all. A good packet is one reading of one sensor:

```
{"sat":"ORB-1","sensor":"batt_v","ts":"2026-03-01T00:00:00Z","v":28.2}
```

Not every packet is good. A few from batch 1:

```
line 9001  {"sat":"ORB-1","sensor":"batt_v","ts":"2026-03-01T05:10:00Z","v":28.1
line 9005  {"sat":"ORB-4","sensor":"panel_t","ts":"2026-03-01T07:00:00Z","v":"n/a"}
line 9009  [1, 2, 3]
line 9010  {"sat":" orb-2 ","sensor":"Wheel_RPM","ts":"2026-03-01T11:55:00Z","v":1990}
```

The first is cut off mid-packet. The second sends the text `"n/a"` instead of a number. The third is valid JSON, but a list, not a packet. The fourth is fine once the spaces and capitals are tidied. Batch 2 even holds a packet whose body is NULL.

### What staging must do

Staging makes **one row per landed packet**, with the packet's fields pulled out into columns, and **judges nothing**. Judging is milestone 3's job. Two promises define it:

1. **Nothing is lost.** For every batch, staged rows = landed rows. A packet that cannot be read at all still gets a row, with its fields NULL and its body kept.
2. **Everything can be traced.** Each row keeps `batch_id` and `line_no`, so any number in any report can be followed back to the exact line it came from. That is [[lineage|lineage]].

**Design choice: no constraints on the parsed columns.** The alternative is to parse straight into a strict table. Then one bad packet either stops the whole batch with an error, or, with `INSERT OR IGNORE`, disappears without a trace. Both are worse than keeping it and saying later what is wrong with it. So `stg_reading` accepts anything; the rules come in the next layer.

### Reading JSON without tripping

You met `json_valid`, `json_type` and `->>` in the JSON lessons. Two facts about them decide how staging is written.

First, `->>` and `json_type` **stop the statement with an error** on text that is not JSON. One cut-off packet would stop staging for the whole batch. So test `json_valid(body)` first. It never errors, and it gives 1 or 0, or NULL for a NULL body.

Second, the test must really come first. In a `WHERE`, SQLite does not promise to look at the conditions of an `AND` in the order you wrote them; the planner may reorder them. `CASE` does promise: it tries each `WHEN` in order and only looks at the `THEN` it picks. So guard with `CASE`:

```sql fragment
CASE WHEN json_valid(body) THEN json_type(body) = 'object' ELSE 0 END
```

For a NULL body, `json_valid` gives NULL, which is not true, so the `ELSE` gives 0. A valid list is not an `'object'`, so it gives 0 too. Compute this once, as `is_object`, and guard every field with it.

### Tidy what is unambiguous

`" orb-2 "` can only mean `ORB-2`. So staging trims and upper-cases the satellite code, and trims and lower-cases the sensor type, matching the forms in the fleet tables. It does not guess beyond that: a satellite code that matches nothing is a question for validation, not a thing to fix.

### Keep the value exactly as sent

`v` may arrive as a number or as text. A column declared `REAL` has **type affinity**: it quietly turns the text `'28.4'` into the number 28.4. Then milestone 3 could never tell that the packet sent a string. So `v_raw` is declared with [[no type at all|affinity]], and keeps each value as it came. `v_type` records `json_type(body, '$.v')`: `'real'`, `'integer'`, `'text'`, `'null'`, or NULL when there is no `v`.

### The pipeline as triggers

Staging has to run once per batch: now for batches 1 to 3, and later for batches that do not exist yet. It has to be re-runnable, and the checks have to be able to run it on a new batch. SQLite has no [[stored procedures|procedures]], so where does "the code that stages batch N" live?

- *Plain statements at the bottom of the script* run once. They cannot be run again for batch 4.
- *A scheduler in another language* would work in production, but moves the logic out of the database and out of reach of the checks.
- **Chosen: command tables and triggers.** Inserting a row into `etl_run` means "run the pipeline for this batch". A trigger on `etl_run` inserts one row per step into `etl_step`, and each step is a trigger `AFTER INSERT ON etl_step WHEN NEW.step = '…'`.

```sql fragment
CREATE TRIGGER etl_some_step AFTER INSERT ON etl_step
WHEN NEW.step = 'some_step'
BEGIN
  ... statements that use NEW.batch_id ...
END;
```

The `WHEN` makes each step trigger fire only for its own step. `NEW` is the step row just inserted, so `NEW.batch_id` is the batch to work on and `NEW.step_id` is the row to record counts in. Later milestones add steps: when `etl_run_steps` inserts several step rows in one multi-row `INSERT`, the triggers [[fire row by row, in order|row-order]], so each step sees the finished work of the one before.

One restriction: a statement inside a trigger cannot *start* with `WITH`. A `WITH` inside a subquery is fine, and milestone 4 will need exactly that.

### Idempotent: running twice changes nothing

Batches get re-run: an operator retries after a crash, or reruns a batch after a fix. A step is **idempotent** when running it twice leaves the database exactly as running it once. For staging, the recipe is *replace, don't add*: delete the batch's staged rows, then insert them again. The delete is keyed on the batch, so other batches are untouched.

**Why this is correct.** After the step runs for batch *b*, staging holds exactly one row per landed packet of *b*: the delete removed every earlier row of *b*, and the insert added one per packet. Running it again starts from any state and ends in that same state, so a second run changes nothing. Other batches' rows are never touched, so the promise holds for every batch at once.

### The run log

Each step writes into its own `etl_step` row what went in and what came out: for staging, `rows_in` is the batch's landed packets and `rows_out` its staged rows. Equal numbers are the first promise, checked on every run. The log turns "did last night's load work?" into a query.

### What it costs

Staging a batch of n packets parses each one once: O(n). But the `DELETE … WHERE batch_id = ?` and the counts must find the batch's rows among every batch ever staged. With no index, each is a full scan of staging: O(N) for N staged rows in total, per step. Here N is 5,410 and it does not matter. At a year of telemetry it would. Milestone 9 reads the query plan and fixes it.

### How to test it

The hand counts are easy to make: packets per batch in the landing zone, and how many bodies are not JSON objects (two in batch 1, one in batch 2, none in batch 3). The test view compares them with staging. The checks also rerun a batch, land a new one, and break staging on purpose.

**Watch out:** `json_valid(body) AND body ->> '$.sat' = 'ORB-1'` works in most quick tests and then fails on the day the planner evaluates the right-hand side first. Guard every JSON read with `CASE WHEN is_object THEN … END`, and compute `is_object` itself with `CASE`.

::: context lineage Following a number back to its source
**Lineage** is the record of where each piece of data came from. Here it is two columns, `batch_id` and `line_no`, carried from staging all the way into the fact table. When an engineer asks why the report shows 99 V on ORB-2, the answer is one query away: the reading came from batch 1, line 9008, and here is the raw packet. Without lineage the only answer is "somewhere in the input". Regulated industries, like aviation and finance, require it.
:::

::: context affinity Type affinity, and a column with no type
SQLite lets any column hold any kind of value, but each column has an **affinity**, a preference taken from its declared type. A column declared `REAL` or `INTEGER` converts text that looks like a number into a number as it is stored, and a `TEXT` column converts numbers into text. A column declared with no type at all has no preference: it stores exactly what it is given, so `typeof(v_raw)` tells you whether the packet sent `28.4` or `"28.4"`. That is the one place in this project where no type is the right type.
:::

::: context procedures What a stored procedure is
A **stored procedure** is a named program kept inside the database, which a client calls with arguments: `CALL stage_batch(4)`. PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle have them. SQLite, which runs inside the program that uses it, leaves that job to the program. The command-table pattern here is a well-known substitute: inserting a row is the call, the row's columns are the arguments, and the triggers are the body. It keeps the logic in SQL, where the checks can run it.
:::

::: context row-order Row triggers and a multi-row insert
A `FOR EACH ROW` trigger, which is what SQLite's triggers are, fires once per row. When one `INSERT` adds several rows, SQLite inserts the first row and runs its `AFTER` triggers to completion, then does the same for the second row, and so on. So three step rows inserted in one statement run the three steps one after another, in the order the rows are listed. The steps never overlap, and each one sees the database exactly as the previous step left it.

   - insert one row per packet of the batch in `landing_packet`, with `batch_id`, `line_no` and `body` copied; `is_object` = 1 when `body` is valid JSON whose `json_type` is `'object'`, and 0 otherwise (a NULL body too); and, only when `is_object` is 1: `sat_code` = the upper-cased, trimmed `sat`, `type_code` = the lower-cased, trimmed `sensor`, `ts_raw` = `ts`, `v_raw` = `v` as read by `->>`, `v_type` = `json_type(body, '$.v')`. Otherwise those five are NULL, and so are `ts`, `sensor_id`, `value` and `reject_reason` for every row;

3. At the end of the script, before the tests, run the pipeline once for every batch in `landing_packet`, oldest first, with one `INSERT … SELECT` into `etl_run`.
4. The test: insert into `expect_count` the rows `('staged', '1', 1382)`, `('staged', '2', 1322)`, `('staged', '3', 2706)`, `('not_object', '1', 2)`, `('not_object', '2', 1)`, `('not_object', '3', 0)`. --- starter
-- =====================================================================
--  ORBIT fleet telemetry warehouse
--
--  One script builds the whole database from an empty file that holds
--  only the landing zone (landing_packet). The layers, in the order the
--  data flows through them:
--
--    1. operational schema   the fleet, as the operations team keeps it
--    2. pipeline control     runs and steps, one trigger per step
--    3. staging              every landed packet, parsed, not trusted
--    4. quarantine           rejected packets, each with one reason
--    5. star schema          dimensions and the fact table
--    6. rollups              hourly and daily aggregates
--    7. trend reports        window functions over the facts
--    8. gaps and islands     outages, empty hours, low-battery streaks
--    9. data quality         checks that must return zero rows
--   10. report suite         what operations reads every morning
--
--  Conventions: times are UTC text 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'; every step can
--  be rerun for the same batch without changing the result.
-- =====================================================================

PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 1. Operational schema: the fleet as the operations team keeps it.
--    Normalised: each fact about the fleet is stored exactly once, and
--    the constraints refuse any row that could not be true.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE satellite (
  sat_id       INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  code         TEXT    NOT NULL UNIQUE CHECK (code GLOB 'ORB-[0-9]*'),
  name         TEXT    NOT NULL,
  launched_on  TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (launched_on IS date(launched_on)),
  status       TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active'
                       CHECK (status IN ('active', 'safe_mode', 'retired')),
  status_since TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (status_since >= launched_on)
);

CREATE TABLE sensor_type (
  type_code  TEXT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY CHECK (type_code = lower(type_code)),
  label      TEXT NOT NULL,
  unit       TEXT NOT NULL,
  min_valid  REAL NOT NULL,
  max_valid  REAL NOT NULL,
  CHECK (min_valid < max_valid)
);

CREATE TABLE sensor (
  sensor_id  INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  sat_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES satellite (sat_id),
  type_code  TEXT    NOT NULL REFERENCES sensor_type (type_code),
  UNIQUE (sat_id, type_code)
);

CREATE TABLE ground_station (
  station_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  code       TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE CHECK (length(code) = 3 AND code = upper(code)),
  name       TEXT NOT NULL,
  latitude   REAL NOT NULL CHECK (latitude BETWEEN -90 AND 90),
  longitude  REAL NOT NULL CHECK (longitude BETWEEN -180 AND 180)
);

-- A planned contact: the satellite is above the station's horizon from
-- aos (acquisition of signal) until los (loss of signal).
CREATE TABLE contact_pass (
  pass_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  sat_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES satellite (sat_id),
  station_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES ground_station (station_id),
  aos        TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (aos IS datetime(aos, '+0 seconds')),
  los        TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (los IS datetime(los, '+0 seconds')),
  CHECK (los > aos),
  UNIQUE (sat_id, aos)
);

-- The one place that turns packet codes into a sensor: which satellite
-- carries which kind of sensor, with the limits that make a value possible.
CREATE VIEW v_sensor_catalog AS
SELECT se.sensor_id,
       sa.sat_id,
       sa.code   AS sat_code,
       sa.status AS sat_status,
       st.type_code,
       st.unit,
       st.min_valid,
       st.max_valid
FROM sensor se
JOIN satellite   sa ON sa.sat_id    = se.sat_id
JOIN sensor_type st ON st.type_code = se.type_code;

-- The roster the operations team reads every morning.
CREATE VIEW v_fleet_roster AS
SELECT sa.code AS sat_code,
       sa.name,
       sa.status,
       COUNT(se.sensor_id) AS sensors,
       COALESCE((SELECT group_concat(type_code, ',')
                 FROM (SELECT type_code FROM sensor
                       WHERE sat_id = sa.sat_id
                       ORDER BY type_code)), '') AS sensor_types,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM contact_pass p WHERE p.sat_id = sa.sat_id) AS passes
FROM satellite sa
LEFT JOIN sensor se ON se.sat_id = sa.sat_id
GROUP BY sa.sat_id
ORDER BY sa.code;

  run_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  batch_id  INTEGER NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE etl_step (
  step_id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  run_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES etl_run (run_id),
  batch_id  INTEGER NOT NULL,
  step      TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (step IN ('stage')),
  rows_in   INTEGER,
  rows_out  INTEGER
);

  sat_code      TEXT,
  type_code     TEXT,
  ts_raw        TEXT,
  v_raw,
  v_type        TEXT,
  -- filled in by the validate step

  sensor_id     INTEGER,
  value         REAL,
  reject_reason TEXT
);

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 12. Known-answer tests. Each expected value below was worked out by
--     hand from the development window's packets, not copied from the
--     pipeline's output. Each test_ view returns the rows where the
--     warehouse disagrees with the hand count: empty means pass.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE expect_count (
  test     TEXT    NOT NULL,
  item     TEXT    NOT NULL,
  expected INTEGER NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (test, item)
);

INSERT INTO expect_count (test, item, expected) VALUES
  ('sensors', 'ORB-1', 4), ('sensors', 'ORB-2', 4), ('sensors', 'ORB-3', 4),
  ('sensors', 'ORB-4', 4), ('sensors', 'ORB-5', 3), ('sensors', 'ORB-6', 4),
  ('passes',  'ORB-1', 6), ('passes',  'ORB-2', 6), ('passes',  'ORB-3', 6),
  ('passes',  'ORB-4', 6), ('passes',  'ORB-5', 6), ('passes',  'ORB-6', 0);

CREATE VIEW test_roster AS
SELECT COALESCE(e.test, a.test) AS test,
       COALESCE(e.item, a.item) AS item,
       e.expected,
       a.actual
FROM (SELECT test, item, expected FROM expect_count
      WHERE test IN ('sensors', 'passes')) e
FULL OUTER JOIN (SELECT 'sensors' AS test, sat_code AS item, sensors AS actual FROM v_fleet_roster
                 UNION ALL
                 SELECT 'passes', sat_code, passes FROM v_fleet_roster) a
  ON a.test = e.test AND a.item = e.item
WHERE e.expected IS NOT a.actual;

-- TODO (milestone 2): the hand counts and the view test_staging.
CREATE VIEW test_staging AS
SELECT NULL AS test, NULL AS item, NULL AS expected, NULL AS actual
WHERE 1;

-- One line per test: how many rows disagree. All zeros is a green build.
CREATE VIEW test_summary AS
SELECT test, failures FROM (
            SELECT 'roster'      AS test, COUNT(*) AS failures FROM test_roster
  UNION ALL SELECT 'staging',            COUNT(*)             FROM test_staging
);

-- The one place that turns packet codes into a sensor: which satellite
-- carries which kind of sensor, with the limits that make a value possible.
CREATE VIEW v_sensor_catalog AS
SELECT se.sensor_id,
       sa.sat_id,
       sa.code   AS sat_code,
       sa.status AS sat_status,
       st.type_code,
       st.unit,
       st.min_valid,
       st.max_valid
FROM sensor se
JOIN satellite   sa ON sa.sat_id    = se.sat_id
JOIN sensor_type st ON st.type_code = se.type_code;

-- The roster the operations team reads every morning.
CREATE VIEW v_fleet_roster AS
SELECT sa.code AS sat_code,
       sa.name,
       sa.status,
       COUNT(se.sensor_id) AS sensors,
       COALESCE((SELECT group_concat(type_code, ',')
                 FROM (SELECT type_code FROM sensor
                       WHERE sat_id = sa.sat_id
                       ORDER BY type_code)), '') AS sensor_types,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM contact_pass p WHERE p.sat_id = sa.sat_id) AS passes
FROM satellite sa
LEFT JOIN sensor se ON se.sat_id = sa.sat_id
GROUP BY sa.sat_id
ORDER BY sa.code;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 2. Pipeline control. SQLite has no stored procedures, so each step is
--    a trigger that fires when a row is added to etl_step. Running the
--    pipeline for a batch is one INSERT INTO etl_run.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE etl_run (
  run_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  batch_id  INTEGER NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE etl_step (
  step_id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  run_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES etl_run (run_id),
  batch_id  INTEGER NOT NULL,
  step      TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (step IN ('stage')),
  rows_in   INTEGER,
  rows_out  INTEGER
);

-- One run is its steps, in order. A multi-row INSERT fires the step
-- triggers row by row, so each step sees the work of the one before.
CREATE TRIGGER etl_run_steps AFTER INSERT ON etl_run
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO etl_step (run_id, batch_id, step) VALUES
    (NEW.run_id, NEW.batch_id, 'stage');
END;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 3. Staging: one row per landed packet, parsed but not yet trusted.
--    No constraints on the parsed columns: staging must accept anything,
--    so that nothing that arrived is ever lost.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE stg_reading (
  batch_id      INTEGER NOT NULL,
  line_no       INTEGER NOT NULL,
  body          TEXT,              -- the packet exactly as it landed
  is_object     INTEGER NOT NULL,  -- 1 when body is a JSON object
  sat_code      TEXT,              -- trimmed, upper case
  type_code     TEXT,              -- trimmed, lower case
  ts_raw        TEXT,
  v_raw,                           -- no type on purpose: keeps 28.4 and '28.4' apart
  v_type        TEXT,              -- json_type of v: 'integer', 'real', 'text', ...
  -- filled in by the validate step
  ts            TEXT,              -- canonical 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS', UTC
  sensor_id     INTEGER,           -- resolved through v_sensor_catalog
  value         REAL,
  reject_reason TEXT               -- NULL when the row passed every rule
);

CREATE TRIGGER etl_stage AFTER INSERT ON etl_step
WHEN NEW.step = 'stage'
BEGIN
  -- Idempotent: a rerun replaces the batch instead of adding to it.
  DELETE FROM stg_reading
  WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id;

  INSERT INTO stg_reading (batch_id, line_no, body, is_object,
                           sat_code, type_code, ts_raw, v_raw, v_type)
  SELECT batch_id,
         line_no,
         body,
         is_object,
         CASE WHEN is_object THEN upper(trim(body ->> '$.sat')) END,
         CASE WHEN is_object THEN lower(trim(body ->> '$.sensor')) END,
         CASE WHEN is_object THEN body ->> '$.ts' END,
         CASE WHEN is_object THEN body ->> '$.v' END,
         CASE WHEN is_object THEN json_type(body, '$.v') END
  FROM (
    SELECT batch_id,
           line_no,
           body,
           -- json_type on text that is not JSON is an error, so test first
           CASE WHEN json_valid(body) THEN json_type(body) = 'object' ELSE 0 END AS is_object
    FROM landing_packet
    WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id
  );

  UPDATE etl_step
  SET rows_in  = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM landing_packet WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id),
      rows_out = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM stg_reading    WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id)
  WHERE step_id = NEW.step_id;
END;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Run the pipeline once for every batch in the landing zone, oldest first.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

INSERT INTO etl_run (batch_id)
SELECT DISTINCT batch_id
FROM landing_packet
ORDER BY batch_id;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 12. Known-answer tests. Each expected value below was worked out by
--     hand from the development window's packets, not copied from the
--     pipeline's output. Each test_ view returns the rows where the
--     warehouse disagrees with the hand count: empty means pass.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE expect_count (
  test     TEXT    NOT NULL,
  item     TEXT    NOT NULL,
  expected INTEGER NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (test, item)
);

INSERT INTO expect_count (test, item, expected) VALUES
  ('sensors', 'ORB-1', 4), ('sensors', 'ORB-2', 4), ('sensors', 'ORB-3', 4),
  ('sensors', 'ORB-4', 4), ('sensors', 'ORB-5', 3), ('sensors', 'ORB-6', 4),
  ('passes',  'ORB-1', 6), ('passes',  'ORB-2', 6), ('passes',  'ORB-3', 6),
  ('passes',  'ORB-4', 6), ('passes',  'ORB-5', 6), ('passes',  'ORB-6', 0);

CREATE VIEW test_roster AS
SELECT COALESCE(e.test, a.test) AS test,
       COALESCE(e.item, a.item) AS item,
       e.expected,
       a.actual
FROM (SELECT test, item, expected FROM expect_count
      WHERE test IN ('sensors', 'passes')) e
FULL OUTER JOIN (SELECT 'sensors' AS test, sat_code AS item, sensors AS actual FROM v_fleet_roster
                 UNION ALL
                 SELECT 'passes', sat_code, passes FROM v_fleet_roster) a
  ON a.test = e.test AND a.item = e.item
WHERE e.expected IS NOT a.actual;

INSERT INTO expect_count (test, item, expected) VALUES
  ('staged', '1', 1382), ('staged', '2', 1322), ('staged', '3', 2706),
  ('not_object', '1', 2), ('not_object', '2', 1), ('not_object', '3', 0);

CREATE VIEW test_staging AS
SELECT COALESCE(e.test, a.test) AS test,
       COALESCE(e.item, a.item) AS item,
       e.expected,
       a.actual
FROM (SELECT test, item, expected FROM expect_count
      WHERE test IN ('staged', 'not_object')) e
FULL OUTER JOIN (SELECT 'staged' AS test, CAST(batch_id AS TEXT) AS item, COUNT(*) AS actual
                 FROM stg_reading GROUP BY batch_id
                 UNION ALL
                 SELECT 'not_object', CAST(batch_id AS TEXT), SUM(NOT is_object)
                 FROM stg_reading GROUP BY batch_id) a
  ON a.test = e.test AND a.item = e.item
WHERE e.expected IS NOT a.actual;

-- One line per test: how many rows disagree. All zeros is a green build.
CREATE VIEW test_summary AS
SELECT test, failures FROM (
            SELECT 'roster'      AS test, COUNT(*) AS failures FROM test_roster
  UNION ALL SELECT 'staging',            COUNT(*)             FROM test_staging
);
--- hint
Write `etl_stage` in three statements: the `DELETE`, the `INSERT … SELECT`, and the `UPDATE etl_step … WHERE step_id = NEW.step_id`. For the insert, compute `is_object` in a subquery in the `FROM`, so the outer `SELECT` can use it to guard each field.
--- hint
The subquery is `SELECT batch_id, line_no, body, CASE WHEN json_valid(body) THEN json_type(body) = 'object' ELSE 0 END AS is_object FROM landing_packet WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id`. Each field is then `CASE WHEN is_object THEN … END`, for example `CASE WHEN is_object THEN upper(trim(body ->> '$.sat')) END`.
--- hint
The driver is `INSERT INTO etl_run (batch_id) SELECT DISTINCT batch_id FROM landing_packet ORDER BY batch_id;`. `test_staging` has the same shape as `test_roster`, with the actual counts from `stg_reading` grouped by `batch_id`: `COUNT(*)` for `'staged'` and `SUM(NOT is_object)` for `'not_object'`.

+++ practice | Pulling fields out of weather packets
--- schema
CREATE TABLE raw_wx (
  line_no INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  body    TEXT
);
INSERT INTO raw_wx VALUES
  (1, '{"station":"svb","temp_c":-12.5,"wind_ms":8}'),
  (2, '{"station":" AWA ","temp_c":11.0,"wind_ms":3}'),
  (3, '{"station":"pun","temp_c":"warm","wind_ms":14}'),
  (4, '{"station":"INU","wind_ms":2}');
--- task
Weather stations send packets like `{"station":"svb","temp_c":-12.5,"wind_ms":8}` into `raw_wx (line_no, body)`. Every body in this table is valid JSON.

Write one `SELECT` that returns one row per packet, ordered by `line_no`, with these columns:

- `line_no`
- `station`: the station code, trimmed and in capitals
- `temp_c`: the `temp_c` value exactly as sent (a number, a text, or NULL when missing)
- `temp_type`: `json_type` of `temp_c`, which is NULL when it is missing
- `wind_ms`: the `wind_ms` value
--- starter
SELECT line_no,
       body ->> '$.station' AS station
FROM raw_wx
ORDER BY line_no;
--- solution
SELECT line_no,
       upper(trim(body ->> '$.station')) AS station,
       body ->> '$.temp_c' AS temp_c,
       json_type(body, '$.temp_c') AS temp_type,
       body ->> '$.wind_ms' AS wind_ms
FROM raw_wx
ORDER BY line_no;
--- hint
`body ->> '$.temp_c'` reads one field as a plain SQL value, and `json_type(body, '$.temp_c')` names its JSON kind: `'real'`, `'integer'`, `'text'`, and so on.
--- hint
The station needs two tidy-ups wrapped around the read: `upper(trim(body ->> '$.station'))`.
--- check result | Four rows: the codes tidied, the text and the missing value kept as they are
ordered
[[1, "SVB", -12.5, "real", 8], [2, "AWA", 11.0, "real", 3], [3, "PUN", "warm", "text", 14], [4, "INU", null, null, 2]]
--- check source | Uses json_type for the kind of temp_c
json_type\s*\(
--- check source absent | Does not hard-code a station
'(SVB|AWA|PUN|INU)'

+++ practice | Rows that are not packets
--- schema
CREATE TABLE raw_cmd (
  line_no INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  body    TEXT
);
INSERT INTO raw_cmd VALUES
  (1, '{"cmd":"wheel_desat","sat":"ORB-2"}'),
  (2, '{"cmd":"reboot","sat":"ORB-4"'),
  (3, NULL),
  (4, '["reboot","ORB-1"]'),
  (5, '{"cmd":"reboot","sat":"ORB-1"}'),
  (6, '42');
--- task
Command acknowledgements land in `raw_cmd (line_no, body)`. Some bodies are cut off, one is NULL, and some are valid JSON that is not an object (a list, a bare number).

Write one `SELECT` that returns every row, ordered by `line_no`, with three columns:

- `line_no`
- `is_object`: 1 when `body` is valid JSON whose `json_type` is `'object'`, and 0 otherwise, including a NULL body
- `cmd`: the `cmd` field when `is_object` is 1, and NULL otherwise

It must not stop with an error on any row.
--- starter
SELECT line_no,
       json_type(body) = 'object' AS is_object,
       body ->> '$.cmd' AS cmd
FROM raw_cmd
ORDER BY line_no;
--- solution
SELECT line_no,
       is_object,
       CASE WHEN is_object THEN body ->> '$.cmd' END AS cmd
FROM (
  SELECT line_no,
         body,
         CASE WHEN json_valid(body) THEN json_type(body) = 'object' ELSE 0 END AS is_object
  FROM raw_cmd
)
ORDER BY line_no;
--- hint
Run the starter: it stops at line 2, because `json_type` errors on text that is not JSON. `json_valid` never errors, so test it first, inside a `CASE`, which only looks at the `THEN` it picks.
--- hint
Compute `is_object` in a subquery as `CASE WHEN json_valid(body) THEN json_type(body) = 'object' ELSE 0 END`, then use `CASE WHEN is_object THEN body ->> '$.cmd' END` outside. A NULL body falls through to the `ELSE 0`.
--- check result | Two real packets, four rows that are not
ordered
[[1, 1, "wheel_desat"], [2, 0, null], [3, 0, null], [4, 0, null], [5, 1, "reboot"], [6, 0, null]]
--- check source | Tests json_valid first
json_valid\s*\(
--- check source | Guards with CASE
[Cc][Aa][Ss][Ee]\s+[Ww][Hh][Ee][Nn]

+++ practice | A staging step you can rerun
--- schema
CREATE TABLE landed (
  batch_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  line_no  INTEGER NOT NULL,
  body     TEXT
);
INSERT INTO landed VALUES
  (1, 1, '{"pump":"P1","psi":41.5}'),
  (1, 2, '{"pump":"P2","psi":39.0}'),
  (2, 1, '{"pump":"P1","psi":42.0}'),
  (2, 2, 'oops'),
  (2, 3, '{"pump":"P3","psi":40.5}');
CREATE TABLE staged (
  batch_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  line_no  INTEGER NOT NULL,
  pump     TEXT,
  psi
);
CREATE TABLE stage_request (
  request_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  batch_id   INTEGER NOT NULL
);
--- task
Pump readings land in `landed (batch_id, line_no, body)`. The tables `staged (batch_id, line_no, pump, psi)` and `stage_request (request_id, batch_id)` exist.

Create the trigger `stage_batch`: after a row is inserted into `stage_request`, stage that row's batch into `staged`, one row per landed line, with `pump` and `psi` read from the body when it is valid JSON and NULL otherwise. Running the same batch twice must leave exactly one staged row per landed line, and must not touch other batches.

Then stage batches 1 and 2 by inserting two rows into `stage_request`.
--- starter

--- solution
CREATE TRIGGER stage_batch AFTER INSERT ON stage_request
BEGIN
  DELETE FROM staged WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id;
  INSERT INTO staged (batch_id, line_no, pump, psi)
  SELECT batch_id,
         line_no,
         CASE WHEN json_valid(body) THEN body ->> '$.pump' END,
         CASE WHEN json_valid(body) THEN body ->> '$.psi' END
  FROM landed
  WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id;
END;

INSERT INTO stage_request (batch_id) VALUES (1), (2);
