+++ practice | The AND that ran the wrong way
--- schema
CREATE TABLE inbox (
  line_no INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  body    TEXT
);
INSERT INTO inbox VALUES
  (1, '{"sat":"ORB-1","kind":"hk"}'),
  (2, '{"sat":"ORB-3","kind":"hk"}'),
  (3, 'ORB-1 partial frame'),
  (4, '{"sat":"ORB-1","kind":"event"}'),
  (5, NULL);
--- task
This view is meant to list the line numbers of ORB-1's packets. It stops with `malformed JSON` on line 3, because it reads the body before testing that the body is JSON:

```sql
CREATE VIEW orb1_lines AS
SELECT line_no
FROM inbox
WHERE body ->> '$.sat' = 'ORB-1' AND json_valid(body);
```

Swapping the two conditions happens to work today, but SQLite does not promise to test the conditions of an `AND` in the order they are written, so a new version or a new index could break it again.

Rewrite `orb1_lines`, keeping its name and its one column, so that it never reads a body that is not valid JSON, whatever order the database chooses.
--- starter
CREATE VIEW orb1_lines AS
SELECT line_no
FROM inbox
WHERE body ->> '$.sat' = 'ORB-1' AND json_valid(body);
--- solution
CREATE VIEW orb1_lines AS
SELECT line_no
FROM inbox
WHERE CASE WHEN json_valid(body) THEN body ->> '$.sat' = 'ORB-1' ELSE 0 END;
--- hint
Only one SQL construct promises the order in which it looks at its parts: `CASE` tries each `WHEN` in turn and evaluates only the `THEN` it picks.
--- hint
Move the whole test into one `CASE`: when the body is valid, the answer is the comparison; otherwise it is 0. `WHERE CASE WHEN json_valid(body) THEN … ELSE 0 END`.
--- check query | Lines 1 and 4 belong to ORB-1
SELECT line_no FROM orb1_lines ORDER BY line_no
=> [[1], [4]]
--- check query | A new packet from ORB-1 shows up
INSERT INTO inbox VALUES (6, '{"sat":"ORB-1","kind":"hk"}');
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orb1_lines
=> [[3]]
--- check source | Guards the read with CASE
[Cc][Aa][Ss][Ee]\s+[Ww][Hh][Ee][Nn]\s+json_valid

+++ practice | A run log for a two-step pipeline
--- schema
CREATE TABLE landed (
  batch_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  line_no  INTEGER NOT NULL,
  body     TEXT
);
INSERT INTO landed VALUES
  (7, 1, '{"tank":"T1","kg":120.5}'),
  (7, 2, 'noise'),
  (7, 3, '{"tank":"T2","kg":98.0}'),
  (8, 1, '{"tank":"T1","kg":119.0}');
CREATE TABLE staged (batch_id INTEGER, line_no INTEGER, tank TEXT, kg REAL);
CREATE TABLE good (batch_id INTEGER, line_no INTEGER, tank TEXT, kg REAL);
CREATE TABLE run (run_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, batch_id INTEGER NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE step (
  step_id  INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  run_id   INTEGER NOT NULL,
  batch_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  name     TEXT NOT NULL,
  rows_in  INTEGER,
  rows_out INTEGER
);
CREATE TRIGGER step_stage AFTER INSERT ON step WHEN NEW.name = 'stage'
BEGIN
  DELETE FROM staged WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id;
  INSERT INTO staged
  SELECT batch_id, line_no,
         CASE WHEN json_valid(body) THEN body ->> '$.tank' END,
         CASE WHEN json_valid(body) THEN body ->> '$.kg' END
  FROM landed WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id;
  UPDATE step SET rows_in = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM landed WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id),
                  rows_out = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM staged WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id)
  WHERE step_id = NEW.step_id;
END;
--- task
A tank-mass pipeline has the tables `landed`, `staged`, `good`, `run (run_id, batch_id)` and `step (step_id, run_id, batch_id, name, rows_in, rows_out)`, and the stage step already exists as the trigger `step_stage`. Two pieces are missing:

1. The trigger `step_keep_good`: after a row is inserted into `step` whose `name` is `'keep_good'`, replace the batch's rows in `good` with its staged rows whose `tank` is not NULL, then set that step row's `rows_in` to the batch's staged rows and `rows_out` to its rows in `good`.
2. The trigger `run_steps`: after a row is inserted into `run`, insert its two steps into `step` in one `INSERT`, `'stage'` first, then `'keep_good'`.

Finally, run batches 7 and 8 by inserting into `run`.
--- starter
CREATE TRIGGER run_steps AFTER INSERT ON run
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO step (run_id, batch_id, name) VALUES
    (NEW.run_id, NEW.batch_id, 'keep_good'),
    (NEW.run_id, NEW.batch_id, 'stage');
END;

INSERT INTO run (batch_id) VALUES (7), (8);
--- solution
CREATE TRIGGER step_keep_good AFTER INSERT ON step WHEN NEW.name = 'keep_good'
BEGIN
  DELETE FROM good WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id;
  INSERT INTO good
  SELECT batch_id, line_no, tank, kg
  FROM staged
  WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id AND tank IS NOT NULL;
  UPDATE step SET rows_in = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM staged WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id),
                  rows_out = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM good WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id)
  WHERE step_id = NEW.step_id;
END;

CREATE TRIGGER run_steps AFTER INSERT ON run
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO step (run_id, batch_id, name) VALUES
    (NEW.run_id, NEW.batch_id, 'stage'),
    (NEW.run_id, NEW.batch_id, 'keep_good');
END;

INSERT INTO run (batch_id) VALUES (7), (8);
--- hint

--- hint
Model `step_keep_good` on `step_stage`: a `DELETE` for the batch, an `INSERT … SELECT` from `staged` with `tank IS NOT NULL`, and an `UPDATE step … WHERE step_id = NEW.step_id`.

=== cap-data-03 | Data system 3: validation and quarantine
--- teach
Last milestone every packet landed in staging, parsed but not judged. This milestone judges them. Each staged row either passes every rule, and goes on to the warehouse, or goes to **quarantine** with the reason it failed.

### What validation must do

**Validation** applies a fixed list of rules to each record. **Quarantine** is the holding area for the records that fail: kept whole, with the reason, where a person can look at them. Message systems call the same idea a [[dead-letter queue|dead-letter]]. Two things are ruled out: loading a bad reading into reports, and throwing it away, which would hide a sensor or a ground station that is going wrong.

The invariant of this layer is a partition, like the one quicksort makes: **every staged row of a batch is exactly one of clean or quarantined**. So for every batch, staged = clean + quarantined, and the quarantined rows are exactly the rows with a reason.

### The rules, in order

Each rejected row gets **exactly one** reason: the first rule it breaks, in this order.

| # | reason | the row is rejected when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `malformed_json` | the body is not a JSON object |
| 2 | `missing_field` | `sat`, `sensor`, `ts` or `v` is missing or null |
| 3 | `bad_timestamp` | `ts` is not a real moment written as `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ` |
| 4 | `non_numeric_value` | `v` is not a JSON number |
| 5 | `unknown_satellite` | no satellite has that code |
| 6 | `unknown_sensor` | the satellite carries no sensor of that type |
| 7 | `out_of_range` | the value is outside the type's `min_valid` to `max_valid` |

The order is not arbitrary. It goes from "cannot read it at all" to "readable, but impossible", and each rule assumes the ones before it passed. The range rule needs a number and a known sensor, so it must come after rules 4 and 6. One reason per row also keeps counting honest: the reasons of a batch add up to its rejects. The price is that a packet with two problems shows only the first; fixing it may reveal the second.

Why keep `unknown_satellite` and `unknown_sensor` apart? Because they have different fixes. An unknown satellite is usually a corrupt packet. An unknown sensor is often a real sensor that nobody has registered yet, and milestone 11 will release those packets automatically when it is.

### Two passes: parse, then judge

The validate step makes two `UPDATE`s over the batch's staged rows.

**Pass 1, parse.** It fills three columns, each NULL when the raw value cannot be used: `ts`, the canonical time; `value`, the number; and `sensor_id`, found through `v_sensor_catalog` by the pair (satellite code, sensor type).

**Pass 2, judge.** One `CASE` walks the rules in order and sets `reject_reason`. A `CASE` stops at its first true `WHEN`, which is exactly "the first rule broken". A row that passes every `WHEN` gets NULL, which means clean.

Parsing first means each value is worked out once, and the `CASE` reads like the table above. Doing it all in one `CASE` would repeat the timestamp test and the lookup in several places.

### Parsing a timestamp safely

`datetime()` reads `'2026-03-01T05:10:00Z'`, with its `T` and `Z`, and rewrites it as `'2026-03-01 05:10:00'`. But it is generous. It rolls 30 February over into March, and without a modifier it copies an hour of `24` straight through. So test with a **round trip** in the packet's own format, through a modifier that forces the date arithmetic:

```sql
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ', '2026-02-30T10:00:00Z', '+0 seconds');
-- 2026-03-02T10:00:00Z   (not the text that arrived: reject)
```

`strftime` writes the moment back in the packet's format. If that equals the text that arrived, the text was a real moment in the right shape. Packet 9004 in batch 1, stamped 30 February, fails here, and so does 9010 in batch 3, stamped `T24:00:00Z`.

### Parsing a number safely

`v` must be a JSON number. The tempting test is a `CAST`:

```sql
SELECT CAST('n/a' AS REAL), CAST('12abc' AS REAL);
-- 0.0, 12.0
```

`CAST` never fails: it takes the number it can find at the start of the text and treats the rest as nothing. A sensor that sends `"n/a"` would read as 0.0 V and look like a dead battery. So the test is on what the packet actually sent: `v_type IN ('integer', 'real')`, the column staging kept for exactly this.

### Quarantine

`quarantine` has one row per rejected packet, keyed by `(batch_id, line_no)`, with the reason, the body as it landed, and `resolved`, a flag the operations team sets once someone has [[looked at the packet|triage]].

Reruns must keep that flag. Suppose someone marked a packet resolved, and then the batch is re-run. Deleting and re-inserting the batch's quarantine rows would wipe the flag. So the step **upserts** instead: `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (batch_id, line_no) DO UPDATE SET reason = …, body = …`, which refreshes the reason and leaves `resolved` alone. And it deletes only the rows that are no longer rejected, which happens when a rule or the fleet changed between runs.

### The whole step

```text
validate(batch b):
  pass 1: for each staged row of b, fill ts, value, sensor_id (NULL if unusable)
  pass 2: for each staged row of b, reject_reason = first rule broken, or NULL
  quarantine: delete b's rows that are no longer rejected;
              upsert b's rejected rows, keeping resolved
  log: rows_in = staged rows of b, rows_out = clean rows of b
```

**Why it is correct.** Pass 2 gives every row exactly one value, a reason or NULL, so the rows split into the two groups. After the two quarantine statements, quarantine holds a row for exactly the rejected rows of b: the delete removed rows that are not rejected, and the upsert added or refreshed one row for each rejected row. So staged = clean + quarantined. Running the step again recomputes the same values from the same staging, so it is idempotent too.

### What it costs

Both passes visit the batch's n rows. For each row, pass 1 finds the sensor by the pair (code, type). `satellite.code` is `UNIQUE` and `sensor (sat_id, type_code)` is `UNIQUE`, so milestone 1 already built the [[B-tree indexes|autoindex]] that make each lookup O(log m) for m sensors. Pass 2's range test finds the limits by `sensor_id`, the primary key: O(log m) again. So the step costs O(n log m), plus finding the batch's rows in staging, which is still a full scan until milestone 9.

### How to test it

The hand count is the list of planted problems: batch 1 has two bad timestamps, two bodies that are not objects, and one each of the other five reasons; batch 2 a NULL body, a packet with no `sat` and a value out of range; batch 3 two bad timestamps, a CPU reading of -80 °C and a sensor type nobody registered. The checks also land new packets that sit exactly on a limit, carry two problems at once, or arrive with a value of `true`.

**Watch out:** a value exactly at a limit is valid: `min_valid` and `max_valid` are the lowest and highest values a sensor can really report, so the test is `value < min_valid OR value > max_valid`, never `<=`. And JSON `true` is not a number, even though `->>` reads it as the integer 1: only `v_type` tells them apart.

::: context dead-letter Where "dead letter" comes from
Post offices had a dead letter office for mail that could be neither delivered nor returned: no readable address, no sender. Clerks opened it to find a clue. Message queues borrowed the name for a side queue where messages that cannot be processed are parked instead of lost. A quarantine table is the same idea in a database: nothing is thrown away, and every parked record says why it is there.
:::

::: context triage Triage, and why the flag must survive
**Triage** means sorting problems by what to do about them, as a hospital sorts patients. Here a person reads a quarantined packet and decides: a corrupt packet to ignore, a sensor to register, a limit that is wrong. Marking it `resolved` records that decision. A pipeline that forgets such marks every time it reruns makes people redo their work, and they soon stop doing it. Keeping human decisions separate from recomputed values is a general rule for any table both people and programs write.
:::

::: context autoindex The indexes your constraints built
When a table has a `UNIQUE` constraint, or a primary key that is not an `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`, SQLite must check every new row against the old ones. It does that with a B-tree index it creates itself, named `sqlite_autoindex_<table>_<n>`. You never wrote `CREATE INDEX`, but the index is there, and the query planner uses it for lookups too. The validate step's sensor lookup rides on two of them. You will see their names in query plans in milestone 9.
:::
--- task
The table `quarantine` and stubs for the trigger `etl_validate` and the view `v_quarantine_summary` are in the starter, and `'validate'` has been added to the steps of a run. Write:

1. The trigger `etl_validate`, which fires after a row is inserted into `etl_step` whose `step` is `'validate'`. For that row's batch:
   - **Parse:** set `ts` to `datetime(ts_raw)` when `strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ', ts_raw, '+0 seconds') = ts_raw`, else NULL; `value` to `v_raw` when `v_type` is `'integer'` or `'real'`, else NULL; `sensor_id` to the `sensor_id` in `v_sensor_catalog` with the row's `sat_code` and `type_code`, else NULL.
   - **Judge:** set `reject_reason` to the first rule broken, in this order: `'malformed_json'` (not `is_object`), `'missing_field'` (any of `sat_code`, `type_code`, `ts_raw`, `v_raw` is NULL), `'bad_timestamp'` (`ts` is NULL), `'non_numeric_value'` (`value` is NULL), `'unknown_satellite'` (no satellite has that `code`), `'unknown_sensor'` (`sensor_id` is NULL), `'out_of_range'` (`value` below the sensor's `min_valid` or above its `max_valid`); otherwise NULL.
   - **Quarantine:** delete the batch's quarantine rows whose line is no longer rejected; then insert one row per rejected line, with its `reason` and `body`, and on a conflict on `(batch_id, line_no)` update only `reason` and `body`.
   - **Log:** set the step row's `rows_in` to the batch's staged rows and `rows_out` to its clean rows.
2. The view `v_quarantine_summary (batch_id, reason, packets)`: how many quarantined packets each batch has for each reason.
3. The test: insert the 13 hand counts into `expect_count` with test `'quarantine'` and item `'<batch>:<reason>'`, for example `('quarantine', '1:bad_timestamp', 2)`. Batch 1: `bad_timestamp` 2, `malformed_json` 2, `missing_field` 1, `non_numeric_value` 1, `out_of_range` 1, `unknown_satellite` 1, `unknown_sensor` 1. Batch 2: `malformed_json` 1, `missing_field` 1, `out_of_range` 1. Batch 3: `bad_timestamp` 2, `out_of_range` 1, `unknown_sensor` 1. Replace the stub `test_quarantine` with a view of the columns `item`, `expected`, `actual` that returns the items where these counts and `v_quarantine_summary` disagree, in either direction.
--- starter
-- =====================================================================
--  ORBIT fleet telemetry warehouse
--
--  One script builds the whole database from an empty file that holds
--  only the landing zone (landing_packet). The layers, in the order the
--  data flows through them:
--
--    1. operational schema   the fleet, as the operations team keeps it
--    2. pipeline control     runs and steps, one trigger per step
--    3. staging              every landed packet, parsed, not trusted
--    4. quarantine           rejected packets, each with one reason
--    5. star schema          dimensions and the fact table
--    6. rollups              hourly and daily aggregates
--    7. trend reports        window functions over the facts
--    8. gaps and islands     outages, empty hours, low-battery streaks
--    9. data quality         checks that must return zero rows
--   10. report suite         what operations reads every morning
--
--  Conventions: times are UTC text 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'; every step can
--  be rerun for the same batch without changing the result.
-- =====================================================================

PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 1. Operational schema: the fleet as the operations team keeps it.
--    Normalised: each fact about the fleet is stored exactly once, and
--    the constraints refuse any row that could not be true.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE satellite (
  sat_id       INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  code         TEXT    NOT NULL UNIQUE CHECK (code GLOB 'ORB-[0-9]*'),
  name         TEXT    NOT NULL,
  launched_on  TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (launched_on IS date(launched_on)),
  status       TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active'
                       CHECK (status IN ('active', 'safe_mode', 'retired')),
  status_since TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (status_since >= launched_on)
);

CREATE TABLE sensor_type (
  type_code  TEXT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY CHECK (type_code = lower(type_code)),
  label      TEXT NOT NULL,
  unit       TEXT NOT NULL,
  min_valid  REAL NOT NULL,
  max_valid  REAL NOT NULL,
  CHECK (min_valid < max_valid)
);

CREATE TABLE sensor (
  sensor_id  INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  sat_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES satellite (sat_id),
  type_code  TEXT    NOT NULL REFERENCES sensor_type (type_code),
  UNIQUE (sat_id, type_code)
);

CREATE TABLE ground_station (
  station_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  code       TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE CHECK (length(code) = 3 AND code = upper(code)),
  name       TEXT NOT NULL,
  latitude   REAL NOT NULL CHECK (latitude BETWEEN -90 AND 90),
  longitude  REAL NOT NULL CHECK (longitude BETWEEN -180 AND 180)
);

-- A planned contact: the satellite is above the station's horizon from
-- aos (acquisition of signal) until los (loss of signal).
CREATE TABLE contact_pass (
  pass_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  sat_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES satellite (sat_id),
  station_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES ground_station (station_id),
  aos        TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (aos IS datetime(aos, '+0 seconds')),
  los        TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (los IS datetime(los, '+0 seconds')),
  CHECK (los > aos),
  UNIQUE (sat_id, aos)
);

-- Reference data. Sensor ids are the satellite number times ten plus a
-- channel, so 23 is ORB-2's flight computer thermometer.
INSERT INTO satellite (sat_id, code, name, launched_on, status, status_since) VALUES
  (1, 'ORB-1', 'Kestrel', '2021-04-12', 'active',  '2021-04-12'),
  (2, 'ORB-2', 'Heron',   '2021-04-12', 'active',  '2021-04-12'),
  (3, 'ORB-3', 'Osprey',  '2022-09-30', 'active',  '2022-09-30'),
  (4, 'ORB-4', 'Plover',  '2023-06-02', 'active',  '2023-06-02'),
  (5, 'ORB-5', 'Swift',   '2024-11-18', 'active',  '2024-11-18'),
  (6, 'ORB-6', 'Tern',    '2019-02-21', 'retired', '2025-08-01');

INSERT INTO sensor_type (type_code, label, unit, min_valid, max_valid) VALUES
  ('batt_v',    'Battery voltage',             'V',    20,    34),
  ('panel_t',   'Solar panel temperature',     'degC', -150,  150),
  ('cpu_t',     'Flight computer temperature', 'degC', -40,   95),
  ('wheel_rpm', 'Reaction wheel speed',        'rpm',  -6000, 6000);

-- The one place that turns packet codes into a sensor: which satellite
-- carries which kind of sensor, with the limits that make a value possible.
CREATE VIEW v_sensor_catalog AS
SELECT se.sensor_id,
       sa.sat_id,
       sa.code   AS sat_code,
       sa.status AS sat_status,
       st.type_code,
       st.unit,
       st.min_valid,
       st.max_valid
FROM sensor se
JOIN satellite   sa ON sa.sat_id    = se.sat_id
JOIN sensor_type st ON st.type_code = se.type_code;

-- The roster the operations team reads every morning.
CREATE VIEW v_fleet_roster AS
SELECT sa.code AS sat_code,
       sa.name,
       sa.status,
       COUNT(se.sensor_id) AS sensors,
       COALESCE((SELECT group_concat(type_code, ',')
                 FROM (SELECT type_code FROM sensor
                       WHERE sat_id = sa.sat_id
                       ORDER BY type_code)), '') AS sensor_types,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM contact_pass p WHERE p.sat_id = sa.sat_id) AS passes
FROM satellite sa
LEFT JOIN sensor se ON se.sat_id = sa.sat_id
GROUP BY sa.sat_id
ORDER BY sa.code;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 2. Pipeline control. SQLite has no stored procedures, so each step is
--    a trigger that fires when a row is added to etl_step. Running the
--    pipeline for a batch is one INSERT INTO etl_run.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE etl_run (
  run_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  batch_id  INTEGER NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE etl_step (
  step_id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  run_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES etl_run (run_id),
  batch_id  INTEGER NOT NULL,
  step      TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (step IN ('stage', 'validate')),
  rows_in   INTEGER,
  rows_out  INTEGER
);

-- One run is its steps, in order. A multi-row INSERT fires the step
-- triggers row by row, so each step sees the work of the one before.
CREATE TRIGGER etl_run_steps AFTER INSERT ON etl_run
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO etl_step (run_id, batch_id, step) VALUES
    (NEW.run_id, NEW.batch_id, 'stage'),
    (NEW.run_id, NEW.batch_id, 'validate');
END;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 3. Staging: one row per landed packet, parsed but not yet trusted.
--    No constraints on the parsed columns: staging must accept anything,
--    so that nothing that arrived is ever lost.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE stg_reading (
  batch_id      INTEGER NOT NULL,
  line_no       INTEGER NOT NULL,
  body          TEXT,              -- the packet exactly as it landed
  is_object     INTEGER NOT NULL,  -- 1 when body is a JSON object
  sat_code      TEXT,              -- trimmed, upper case
  type_code     TEXT,              -- trimmed, lower case
  ts_raw        TEXT,
  v_raw,                           -- no type on purpose: keeps 28.4 and '28.4' apart
  v_type        TEXT,              -- json_type of v: 'integer', 'real', 'text', ...
  -- filled in by the validate step
  ts            TEXT,              -- canonical 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS', UTC
  sensor_id     INTEGER,           -- resolved through v_sensor_catalog
  value         REAL,
  reject_reason TEXT               -- NULL when the row passed every rule
);

CREATE TRIGGER etl_stage AFTER INSERT ON etl_step
WHEN NEW.step = 'stage'
BEGIN
  -- Idempotent: a rerun replaces the batch instead of adding to it.
  DELETE FROM stg_reading
  WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id;

  INSERT INTO stg_reading (batch_id, line_no, body, is_object,
                           sat_code, type_code, ts_raw, v_raw, v_type)
  SELECT batch_id,
         line_no,
         body,
         is_object,
         CASE WHEN is_object THEN upper(trim(body ->> '$.sat')) END,
         CASE WHEN is_object THEN lower(trim(body ->> '$.sensor')) END,
         CASE WHEN is_object THEN body ->> '$.ts' END,
         CASE WHEN is_object THEN body ->> '$.v' END,
         CASE WHEN is_object THEN json_type(body, '$.v') END
  FROM (
    SELECT batch_id,
           line_no,
           body,
           -- json_type on text that is not JSON is an error, so test first
           CASE WHEN json_valid(body) THEN json_type(body) = 'object' ELSE 0 END AS is_object
    FROM landing_packet
    WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id
  );

  UPDATE etl_step
  SET rows_in  = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM landing_packet WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id),
      rows_out = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM stg_reading    WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id)
  WHERE step_id = NEW.step_id;
END;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 4. Validation and quarantine (milestone 3).
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE quarantine (
  batch_id  INTEGER NOT NULL,
  line_no   INTEGER NOT NULL,
  reason    TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (reason IN (
              'malformed_json', 'missing_field', 'bad_timestamp', 'non_numeric_value',
              'unknown_satellite', 'unknown_sensor', 'out_of_range')),
  body      TEXT,
  resolved  INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (resolved IN (0, 1)),
  PRIMARY KEY (batch_id, line_no)
);

CREATE TRIGGER etl_validate AFTER INSERT ON etl_step
WHEN NEW.step = 'validate'
BEGIN
  SELECT 'TODO: parse, judge, quarantine, count';
END;

CREATE VIEW v_quarantine_summary AS
SELECT NULL AS batch_id, NULL AS reason, NULL AS packets
WHERE 0;  -- TODO

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Run the pipeline once for every batch in the landing zone, oldest first.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

INSERT INTO etl_run (batch_id)
SELECT DISTINCT batch_id
FROM landing_packet
ORDER BY batch_id;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 12. Known-answer tests. Each expected value below was worked out by
--     hand from the development window's packets, not copied from the
--     pipeline's output. Each test_ view returns the rows where the
--     warehouse disagrees with the hand count: empty means pass.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE expect_count (
  test     TEXT    NOT NULL,
  item     TEXT    NOT NULL,
  expected INTEGER NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (test, item)
);

INSERT INTO expect_count (test, item, expected) VALUES
  ('sensors', 'ORB-1', 4), ('sensors', 'ORB-2', 4), ('sensors', 'ORB-3', 4),
  ('sensors', 'ORB-4', 4), ('sensors', 'ORB-5', 3), ('sensors', 'ORB-6', 4),
  ('passes',  'ORB-1', 6), ('passes',  'ORB-2', 6), ('passes',  'ORB-3', 6),
  ('passes',  'ORB-4', 6), ('passes',  'ORB-5', 6), ('passes',  'ORB-6', 0);

CREATE VIEW test_roster AS
SELECT COALESCE(e.test, a.test) AS test,
       COALESCE(e.item, a.item) AS item,
       e.expected,
       a.actual
FROM (SELECT test, item, expected FROM expect_count
      WHERE test IN ('sensors', 'passes')) e
FULL OUTER JOIN (SELECT 'sensors' AS test, sat_code AS item, sensors AS actual FROM v_fleet_roster
                 UNION ALL
                 SELECT 'passes', sat_code, passes FROM v_fleet_roster) a
  ON a.test = e.test AND a.item = e.item
WHERE e.expected IS NOT a.actual;

INSERT INTO expect_count (test, item, expected) VALUES
  ('staged', '1', 1382), ('staged', '2', 1322), ('staged', '3', 2706),
  ('not_object', '1', 2), ('not_object', '2', 1), ('not_object', '3', 0);

CREATE VIEW test_staging AS
SELECT COALESCE(e.test, a.test) AS test,
       COALESCE(e.item, a.item) AS item,
       e.expected,
       a.actual
FROM (SELECT test, item, expected FROM expect_count
      WHERE test IN ('staged', 'not_object')) e
FULL OUTER JOIN (SELECT 'staged' AS test, CAST(batch_id AS TEXT) AS item, COUNT(*) AS actual
                 FROM stg_reading GROUP BY batch_id
                 UNION ALL
                 SELECT 'not_object', CAST(batch_id AS TEXT), SUM(NOT is_object)
                 FROM stg_reading GROUP BY batch_id) a
  ON a.test = e.test AND a.item = e.item
WHERE e.expected IS NOT a.actual;

-- TODO (milestone 3): the hand counts and the view test_quarantine.
CREATE VIEW test_quarantine AS
SELECT NULL AS item, NULL AS expected, NULL AS actual
WHERE 1;

-- One line per test: how many rows disagree. All zeros is a green build.
CREATE VIEW test_summary AS
SELECT test, failures FROM (
            SELECT 'roster'      AS test, COUNT(*) AS failures FROM test_roster
  UNION ALL SELECT 'staging',            COUNT(*)             FROM test_staging
  UNION ALL SELECT 'quarantine',         COUNT(*)             FROM test_quarantine
);
--- solution
-- =====================================================================
--  ORBIT fleet telemetry warehouse
--
--  One script builds the whole database from an empty file that holds
--  only the landing zone (landing_packet). The layers, in the order the
--  data flows through them:
--
--    1. operational schema   the fleet, as the operations team keeps it
--    2. pipeline control     runs and steps, one trigger per step
--    3. staging              every landed packet, parsed, not trusted
--    4. quarantine           rejected packets, each with one reason
--    5. star schema          dimensions and the fact table
--    6. rollups              hourly and daily aggregates
--    7. trend reports        window functions over the facts
--    8. gaps and islands     outages, empty hours, low-battery streaks
--    9. data quality         checks that must return zero rows
--   10. report suite         what operations reads every morning
--
--  Conventions: times are UTC text 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'; every step can
--  be rerun for the same batch without changing the result.
-- =====================================================================

PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 1. Operational schema: the fleet as the operations team keeps it.
--    Normalised: each fact about the fleet is stored exactly once, and
--    the constraints refuse any row that could not be true.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE satellite (
  sat_id       INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  code         TEXT    NOT NULL UNIQUE CHECK (code GLOB 'ORB-[0-9]*'),
  name         TEXT    NOT NULL,
  launched_on  TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (launched_on IS date(launched_on)),
  status       TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active'
                       CHECK (status IN ('active', 'safe_mode', 'retired')),
  status_since TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (status_since >= launched_on)
);

CREATE TABLE sensor_type (
  type_code  TEXT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY CHECK (type_code = lower(type_code)),
  label      TEXT NOT NULL,
  unit       TEXT NOT NULL,
  min_valid  REAL NOT NULL,
  max_valid  REAL NOT NULL,
  CHECK (min_valid < max_valid)
);

CREATE TABLE sensor (
  sensor_id  INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  sat_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES satellite (sat_id),
  type_code  TEXT    NOT NULL REFERENCES sensor_type (type_code),
  UNIQUE (sat_id, type_code)
);

CREATE TABLE ground_station (
  station_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  code       TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE CHECK (length(code) = 3 AND code = upper(code)),
  name       TEXT NOT NULL,
  latitude   REAL NOT NULL CHECK (latitude BETWEEN -90 AND 90),
  longitude  REAL NOT NULL CHECK (longitude BETWEEN -180 AND 180)
);

-- A planned contact: the satellite is above the station's horizon from
-- aos (acquisition of signal) until los (loss of signal).
CREATE TABLE contact_pass (
  pass_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  sat_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES satellite (sat_id),
  station_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES ground_station (station_id),
  aos        TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (aos IS datetime(aos, '+0 seconds')),
  los        TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (los IS datetime(los, '+0 seconds')),
  CHECK (los > aos),
  UNIQUE (sat_id, aos)
);

-- The one place that turns packet codes into a sensor: which satellite
-- carries which kind of sensor, with the limits that make a value possible.
CREATE VIEW v_sensor_catalog AS
SELECT se.sensor_id,
       sa.sat_id,
       sa.code   AS sat_code,
       sa.status AS sat_status,
       st.type_code,
       st.unit,
       st.min_valid,
       st.max_valid
FROM sensor se
JOIN satellite   sa ON sa.sat_id    = se.sat_id
JOIN sensor_type st ON st.type_code = se.type_code;

-- The roster the operations team reads every morning.
CREATE VIEW v_fleet_roster AS
SELECT sa.code AS sat_code,
       sa.name,
       sa.status,
       COUNT(se.sensor_id) AS sensors,
       COALESCE((SELECT group_concat(type_code, ',')
                 FROM (SELECT type_code FROM sensor
                       WHERE sat_id = sa.sat_id
                       ORDER BY type_code)), '') AS sensor_types,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM contact_pass p WHERE p.sat_id = sa.sat_id) AS passes
FROM satellite sa
LEFT JOIN sensor se ON se.sat_id = sa.sat_id
GROUP BY sa.sat_id
ORDER BY sa.code;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 2. Pipeline control. SQLite has no stored procedures, so each step is
--    a trigger that fires when a row is added to etl_step. Running the
--    pipeline for a batch is one INSERT INTO etl_run.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE etl_run (
  run_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  batch_id  INTEGER NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE etl_step (
  step_id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  run_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES etl_run (run_id),
  batch_id  INTEGER NOT NULL,
  step      TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (step IN ('stage', 'validate')),
  rows_in   INTEGER,
  rows_out  INTEGER
);

-- One run is its steps, in order. A multi-row INSERT fires the step
-- triggers row by row, so each step sees the work of the one before.
CREATE TRIGGER etl_run_steps AFTER INSERT ON etl_run
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO etl_step (run_id, batch_id, step) VALUES
    (NEW.run_id, NEW.batch_id, 'stage'),
    (NEW.run_id, NEW.batch_id, 'validate');
END;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 3. Staging: one row per landed packet, parsed but not yet trusted.
--    No constraints on the parsed columns: staging must accept anything,
--    so that nothing that arrived is ever lost.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE stg_reading (
  batch_id      INTEGER NOT NULL,
  line_no       INTEGER NOT NULL,
  body          TEXT,              -- the packet exactly as it landed
  is_object     INTEGER NOT NULL,  -- 1 when body is a JSON object
  sat_code      TEXT,              -- trimmed, upper case
  type_code     TEXT,              -- trimmed, lower case
  ts_raw        TEXT,
  v_raw,                           -- no type on purpose: keeps 28.4 and '28.4' apart
  v_type        TEXT,              -- json_type of v: 'integer', 'real', 'text', ...
  -- filled in by the validate step
  ts            TEXT,              -- canonical 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS', UTC
  sensor_id     INTEGER,           -- resolved through v_sensor_catalog
  value         REAL,
  reject_reason TEXT               -- NULL when the row passed every rule
);

CREATE TRIGGER etl_stage AFTER INSERT ON etl_step
WHEN NEW.step = 'stage'
BEGIN
  -- Idempotent: a rerun replaces the batch instead of adding to it.
  DELETE FROM stg_reading
  WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id;

  INSERT INTO stg_reading (batch_id, line_no, body, is_object,
                           sat_code, type_code, ts_raw, v_raw, v_type)
  SELECT batch_id,
         line_no,
         body,
         is_object,
         CASE WHEN is_object THEN upper(trim(body ->> '$.sat')) END,
         CASE WHEN is_object THEN lower(trim(body ->> '$.sensor')) END,
         CASE WHEN is_object THEN body ->> '$.ts' END,
         CASE WHEN is_object THEN body ->> '$.v' END,
         CASE WHEN is_object THEN json_type(body, '$.v') END
  FROM (
    SELECT batch_id,
           line_no,
           body,
           -- json_type on text that is not JSON is an error, so test first
           CASE WHEN json_valid(body) THEN json_type(body) = 'object' ELSE 0 END AS is_object
    FROM landing_packet
    WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id
  );

  UPDATE etl_step
  SET rows_in  = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM landing_packet WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id),
      rows_out = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM stg_reading    WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id)
  WHERE step_id = NEW.step_id;
END;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 4. Validation and quarantine. Every staged row either passes every
--    rule or is quarantined with exactly one reason: the first rule it
--    breaks, in the order the validate step checks them.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE quarantine (
  batch_id  INTEGER NOT NULL,
  line_no   INTEGER NOT NULL,
  reason    TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (reason IN (
              'malformed_json', 'missing_field', 'bad_timestamp', 'non_numeric_value',
              'unknown_satellite', 'unknown_sensor', 'out_of_range')),
  body      TEXT,
  resolved  INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (resolved IN (0, 1)),
  PRIMARY KEY (batch_id, line_no)
);

CREATE TRIGGER etl_validate AFTER INSERT ON etl_step
WHEN NEW.step = 'validate'
BEGIN
  -- Pass 1: parse. Each column stays NULL when its raw value cannot be used.
  UPDATE stg_reading
  -- The round trip goes through '+0 seconds' so SQLite does the date
  -- arithmetic: without a modifier it lets a time like 24:30 through.
  SET ts        = CASE WHEN strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ', ts_raw, '+0 seconds') = ts_raw
                       THEN datetime(ts_raw) END,
      value     = CASE WHEN v_type IN ('integer', 'real') THEN v_raw END,
      sensor_id = (SELECT c.sensor_id
                   FROM v_sensor_catalog c
                   WHERE c.sat_code  = stg_reading.sat_code
                     AND c.type_code = stg_reading.type_code)
  WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id;

  -- Pass 2: judge. The first rule broken is the reason; NULL means clean.
  UPDATE stg_reading
  SET reject_reason = CASE
        WHEN NOT is_object THEN 'malformed_json'
        WHEN sat_code IS NULL OR type_code IS NULL
          OR ts_raw IS NULL OR v_raw IS NULL THEN 'missing_field'
        WHEN ts IS NULL THEN 'bad_timestamp'
        WHEN value IS NULL THEN 'non_numeric_value'
        WHEN NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM satellite s WHERE s.code = stg_reading.sat_code)
          THEN 'unknown_satellite'
        WHEN sensor_id IS NULL THEN 'unknown_sensor'
        WHEN value < (SELECT c.min_valid FROM v_sensor_catalog c
                      WHERE c.sensor_id = stg_reading.sensor_id)
          OR value > (SELECT c.max_valid FROM v_sensor_catalog c
                      WHERE c.sensor_id = stg_reading.sensor_id)
          THEN 'out_of_range'
      END
  WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id;

  -- Quarantine the rejects. A rerun refreshes the reason but keeps the
  -- triage flag someone may already have set.
  DELETE FROM quarantine
  WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id
    AND line_no NOT IN (SELECT line_no
                        FROM stg_reading
                        WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id
                          AND reject_reason IS NOT NULL);

  INSERT INTO quarantine (batch_id, line_no, reason, body)
  SELECT batch_id, line_no, reject_reason, body
  FROM stg_reading
  WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id
    AND reject_reason IS NOT NULL
  ON CONFLICT (batch_id, line_no) DO UPDATE SET
    reason = excluded.reason,
    body   = excluded.body;

  UPDATE etl_step
  SET rows_in  = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM stg_reading WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id),
      rows_out = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM stg_reading
                  WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id AND reject_reason IS NULL)
  WHERE step_id = NEW.step_id;
END;

-- Rejects per batch and reason: the first thing to read after a load.
CREATE VIEW v_quarantine_summary AS
SELECT batch_id,
       reason,
       COUNT(*) AS packets
FROM quarantine
GROUP BY batch_id, reason;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Run the pipeline once for every batch in the landing zone, oldest first.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

INSERT INTO etl_run (batch_id)
SELECT DISTINCT batch_id
FROM landing_packet
ORDER BY batch_id;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 12. Known-answer tests. Each expected value below was worked out by
--     hand from the development window's packets, not copied from the
--     pipeline's output. Each test_ view returns the rows where the
--     warehouse disagrees with the hand count: empty means pass.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE expect_count (
  test     TEXT    NOT NULL,
  item     TEXT    NOT NULL,
  expected INTEGER NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (test, item)
);

INSERT INTO expect_count (test, item, expected) VALUES

  ('sensors', 'ORB-4', 4), ('sensors', 'ORB-5', 3), ('sensors', 'ORB-6', 4),
  ('passes',  'ORB-1', 6), ('passes',  'ORB-2', 6), ('passes',  'ORB-3', 6),
  ('passes',  'ORB-4', 6), ('passes',  'ORB-5', 6), ('passes',  'ORB-6', 0);

CREATE VIEW test_roster AS
SELECT COALESCE(e.test, a.test) AS test,
       COALESCE(e.item, a.item) AS item,
       e.expected,
       a.actual
FROM (SELECT test, item, expected FROM expect_count
      WHERE test IN ('sensors', 'passes')) e
FULL OUTER JOIN (SELECT 'sensors' AS test, sat_code AS item, sensors AS actual FROM v_fleet_roster
                 UNION ALL
                 SELECT 'passes', sat_code, passes FROM v_fleet_roster) a
  ON a.test = e.test AND a.item = e.item
WHERE e.expected IS NOT a.actual;

  ('not_object', '1', 2), ('not_object', '2', 1), ('not_object', '3', 0);

CREATE VIEW test_staging AS
SELECT COALESCE(e.test, a.test) AS test,
       COALESCE(e.item, a.item) AS item,
       e.expected,
       a.actual
FROM (SELECT test, item, expected FROM expect_count
      WHERE test IN ('staged', 'not_object')) e
FULL OUTER JOIN (SELECT 'staged' AS test, CAST(batch_id AS TEXT) AS item, COUNT(*) AS actual
                 FROM stg_reading GROUP BY batch_id
                 UNION ALL
                 SELECT 'not_object', CAST(batch_id AS TEXT), SUM(NOT is_object)
                 FROM stg_reading GROUP BY batch_id) a
  ON a.test = e.test AND a.item = e.item
WHERE e.expected IS NOT a.actual;

       e.expected,

-- One line per test: how many rows disagree. All zeros is a green build.
CREATE VIEW test_summary AS
SELECT test, failures FROM (
            SELECT 'roster'      AS test, COUNT(*) AS failures FROM test_roster
  UNION ALL SELECT 'staging',            COUNT(*)             FROM test_staging
  UNION ALL SELECT 'quarantine',         COUNT(*)             FROM test_quarantine
);
--- hint
Write pass 1 as one `UPDATE stg_reading SET ts = …, value = …, sensor_id = (SELECT …) WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id`. Inside the subquery, refer to the row being updated as `stg_reading.sat_code`, so it is not confused with the catalog's own `sat_code`.
--- hint
Pass 2 is `UPDATE stg_reading SET reject_reason = CASE WHEN NOT is_object THEN 'malformed_json' WHEN … END WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id`. The unknown-satellite test is `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM satellite s WHERE s.code = stg_reading.sat_code)`, and the range test reads `min_valid` and `max_valid` from `v_sensor_catalog` by `sensor_id`.
--- hint
The quarantine delete keeps the rows whose line is still rejected: `DELETE FROM quarantine WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id AND line_no NOT IN (SELECT line_no FROM stg_reading WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id AND reject_reason IS NOT NULL)`. The insert ends with `ON CONFLICT (batch_id, line_no) DO UPDATE SET reason = excluded.reason, body = excluded.body`.

+++ practice | Antenna logs: the first rule broken
--- schema
CREATE TABLE antenna (antenna_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, max_elev REAL NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO antenna VALUES ('A1', 90), ('A2', 85);
CREATE TABLE stg_point (
  line_no    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  antenna_id TEXT,
  elev_raw,
  elev_type  TEXT
);
INSERT INTO stg_point VALUES
  (1, 'A1', 45.5, 'real'),
  (2, NULL, 10, 'integer'),
  (3, 'A9', 20, 'integer'),
  (4, 'A2', 'high', 'text'),
  (5, 'A2', 86, 'integer'),
  (6, 'A1', -1, 'integer'),
  (7, 'A1', 90, 'integer'),
  (8, 'A9', NULL, NULL);
--- task
Antenna pointing logs are staged in `stg_point (line_no, antenna_id, elev_raw, elev_type)`; `elev_type` is the JSON type the elevation arrived as. The antennas are in `antenna (antenna_id, max_elev)`.

Create the view `point_reasons (line_no, reason)` with one row per staged row, where `reason` is the **first** rule the row breaks, in this order, or NULL when it breaks none:

1. `'missing_field'`: `antenna_id` or `elev_raw` is NULL
2. `'non_numeric'`: `elev_type` is not `'integer'` or `'real'`
3. `'unknown_antenna'`: no antenna has that id
4. `'out_of_range'`: the elevation is below 0 or above that antenna's `max_elev`
--- starter
CREATE VIEW point_reasons AS
SELECT line_no,
       CASE
         WHEN elev_raw < 0 THEN 'out_of_range'
         WHEN antenna_id IS NULL THEN 'missing_field'
       END AS reason
FROM stg_point;
--- solution
CREATE VIEW point_reasons AS
SELECT line_no,
       CASE
         WHEN antenna_id IS NULL OR elev_raw IS NULL THEN 'missing_field'
         WHEN elev_type NOT IN ('integer', 'real') THEN 'non_numeric'
         WHEN NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM antenna a WHERE a.antenna_id = p.antenna_id) THEN 'unknown_antenna'
         WHEN elev_raw < 0
           OR elev_raw > (SELECT a.max_elev FROM antenna a WHERE a.antenna_id = p.antenna_id)
           THEN 'out_of_range'
       END AS reason
FROM stg_point p;
--- hint
A `CASE` stops at the first `WHEN` that is true, so write the `WHEN`s in the order of the rules. A row that passes them all gets NULL, because there is no `ELSE`.
--- hint
The antenna rules need the antenna table: `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM antenna a WHERE a.antenna_id = p.antenna_id)`, and `(SELECT a.max_elev FROM antenna a WHERE a.antenna_id = p.antenna_id)` for the upper limit. Line 8 breaks two rules; only the first counts.
--- check query | One reason per line, the first rule broken
SELECT line_no, reason FROM point_reasons ORDER BY line_no
=> [[1, null], [2, "missing_field"], [3, "unknown_antenna"], [4, "non_numeric"], [5, "out_of_range"], [6, "out_of_range"], [7, null], [8, "missing_field"]]
--- check query | 90 on A1 is on the limit, so it is clean; -1 is not
SELECT line_no, reason FROM point_reasons WHERE line_no IN (6, 7) ORDER BY line_no
=> [[6, "out_of_range"], [7, null]]
--- check query | Line 8 breaks two rules and shows only the first
SELECT reason FROM point_reasons WHERE line_no = 8
=> [["missing_field"]]
--- check query | A new antenna makes its lines known
INSERT INTO antenna VALUES ('A9', 80);
SELECT line_no, reason FROM point_reasons WHERE line_no IN (3, 8) ORDER BY line_no
=> [[3, null], [8, "missing_field"]]

+++ practice | Every reason on the dashboard, even the zeros
--- schema
CREATE TABLE quarantine (
  batch_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  line_no  INTEGER NOT NULL,
  reason   TEXT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (batch_id, line_no)
);
INSERT INTO quarantine VALUES
  (1, 4, 'bad_timestamp'), (1, 9, 'malformed_json'), (1, 12, 'bad_timestamp'),
  (2, 3, 'out_of_range'), (2, 8, 'malformed_json'), (2, 11, 'malformed_json');
--- task
The quarantine dashboard shows one tile per reason, and a tile must show 0 rather than disappear. The possible reasons are `'malformed_json'`, `'missing_field'`, `'bad_timestamp'`, `'out_of_range'`.

Create the view `reason_tiles (reason, batch_1, batch_2, total)` with one row for **each of the four reasons**, ordered by `reason`: how many packets of batch 1, of batch 2, and of both are in `quarantine (batch_id, line_no, reason)` with that reason. Zeros are 0, not NULL.
--- starter
CREATE VIEW reason_tiles AS
SELECT reason,
       SUM(batch_id = 1) AS batch_1,
       SUM(batch_id = 2) AS batch_2,
       COUNT(*) AS total
FROM quarantine
GROUP BY reason
ORDER BY reason;
--- solution
CREATE VIEW reason_tiles AS
SELECT r.reason,
       COALESCE(SUM(q.batch_id = 1), 0) AS batch_1,
       COALESCE(SUM(q.batch_id = 2), 0) AS batch_2,
       COUNT(q.line_no) AS total
FROM (SELECT 'malformed_json' AS reason
      UNION ALL SELECT 'missing_field'
      UNION ALL SELECT 'bad_timestamp'
      UNION ALL SELECT 'out_of_range') r
LEFT JOIN quarantine q ON q.reason = r.reason
GROUP BY r.reason
ORDER BY r.reason;
--- hint
A reason with no packets has no rows in `quarantine`, so no `GROUP BY` over `quarantine` can produce it. Start from a list of all four reasons, and `LEFT JOIN` the quarantine rows to it.
--- hint
`FROM (SELECT 'malformed_json' AS reason UNION ALL SELECT 'missing_field' UNION ALL …) r LEFT JOIN quarantine q ON q.reason = r.reason`. For a reason with no match, `SUM` gives NULL, so wrap it in `COALESCE(…, 0)`, and count `q.line_no` rather than `*`.
--- check query | Four tiles, missing_field at 0
SELECT * FROM reason_tiles
=> [["bad_timestamp", 2, 0, 2], ["malformed_json", 1, 2, 3], ["missing_field", 0, 0, 0], ["out_of_range", 0, 1, 1]]
--- check query | No NULLs anywhere
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM reason_tiles WHERE batch_1 IS NULL OR batch_2 IS NULL OR total IS NULL
=> [[0]]
--- check query | A new reject shows up on its tile

=> [[1, 1]]

+++ practice | Split a batch into clean and quarantined
--- schema
CREATE TABLE stg (
  batch_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  line_no  INTEGER NOT NULL,
  body     TEXT,
  reason   TEXT
);
INSERT INTO stg VALUES
  (5, 1, '{"k":1}', NULL), (5, 2, 'bad', 'malformed_json'), (5, 3, '{"k":3}', NULL),
  (5, 4, '{"x":4}', 'missing_field'), (6, 1, '{"k":5}', NULL), (6, 2, 'oops', 'malformed_json');
CREATE TABLE clean (batch_id INTEGER, line_no INTEGER, body TEXT, PRIMARY KEY (batch_id, line_no));
CREATE TABLE quarantine (
  batch_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  line_no  INTEGER NOT NULL,
  reason   TEXT NOT NULL,
  body     TEXT,
  PRIMARY KEY (batch_id, line_no)
);
--- task
The staged rows in `stg (batch_id, line_no, body, reason)` are already judged: `reason` is NULL for a clean row.

1. Copy every clean row into `clean (batch_id, line_no, body)` and every rejected row into `quarantine (batch_id, line_no, reason, body)`.
2. Create the view `split_check (batch_id, staged, clean, quarantined, ok)` with one row per batch in `stg`, ordered by `batch_id`, where `ok` is 1 when staged = clean + quarantined, and 0 otherwise.
--- starter
INSERT INTO clean (batch_id, line_no, body)
SELECT batch_id, line_no, body FROM stg;

CREATE VIEW split_check AS
SELECT batch_id, COUNT(*) AS staged, 0 AS clean, 0 AS quarantined, 0 AS ok
FROM stg
GROUP BY batch_id;
--- solution
INSERT INTO clean (batch_id, line_no, body)
SELECT batch_id, line_no, body FROM stg WHERE reason IS NULL;

INSERT INTO quarantine (batch_id, line_no, reason, body)
SELECT batch_id, line_no, reason, body FROM stg WHERE reason IS NOT NULL;

CREATE VIEW split_check AS
SELECT s.batch_id,
       s.staged,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM clean c WHERE c.batch_id = s.batch_id) AS clean,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM quarantine q WHERE q.batch_id = s.batch_id) AS quarantined,
       s.staged = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM clean c WHERE c.batch_id = s.batch_id)
                + (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM quarantine q WHERE q.batch_id = s.batch_id) AS ok
FROM (SELECT batch_id, COUNT(*) AS staged FROM stg GROUP BY batch_id) s
ORDER BY s.batch_id;
--- hint
Two `INSERT … SELECT`s from `stg`, one with `WHERE reason IS NULL` and one with `WHERE reason IS NOT NULL`, so every row goes to exactly one place.
--- hint
Count the staged rows per batch in a subquery, and count `clean` and `quarantine` for the same batch with correlated subqueries. `ok` is the comparison itself, which gives 1 or 0.
--- check query | Both batches split correctly
SELECT * FROM split_check
=> [[5, 4, 2, 2, 1], [6, 2, 1, 1, 1]]
--- check query | The rejected rows kept their reasons and bodies
SELECT batch_id, line_no, reason, body FROM quarantine ORDER BY batch_id, line_no
=> [[5, 2, "malformed_json", "bad"], [5, 4, "missing_field", "{\"x\":4}"], [6, 2, "malformed_json", "oops"]]
--- check query | The check notices a row that went missing
DELETE FROM clean WHERE batch_id = 6;
SELECT batch_id, ok FROM split_check
=> [[5, 1], [6, 0]]

+++ practice | Moments that are not moments
--- schema
CREATE TABLE stamps (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, raw TEXT);
INSERT INTO stamps VALUES
  (1, '2026-03-01T10:00:00Z'),
  (2, '2026-02-29T10:00:00Z'),
  (3, '2028-02-29T10:00:00Z'),
  (4, '2026-03-01T24:00:00Z'),
  (5, '2026-03-01T10:00:00'),
  (6, '2026-03-01 10:00:00Z'),
  (7, '2026-03-01T10:00:00.250Z'),
  (8, '2026-03-01T23:59:59Z'),
  (9, NULL);
--- task
Timestamps arrive in `stamps (id, raw)`. A timestamp is valid only when it is a real moment written **exactly** as `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ`.

Create the view `stamp_check (id, ok, ts)` with one row per stamp: `ok` is 1 when `raw` is valid and 0 otherwise, including NULL; `ts` is the moment as `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS` when valid, and NULL otherwise.

Watch the traps: 29 February 2026 does not exist, but 29 February 2028 does; `24:00:00` is not a time of day; the `T`, the `Z` and whole seconds are all required.
--- starter
CREATE VIEW stamp_check AS
SELECT id,
       datetime(raw) IS NOT NULL AS ok,
       datetime(raw) AS ts
FROM stamps;
--- solution
CREATE VIEW stamp_check AS
SELECT id,
       COALESCE(strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ', raw, '+0 seconds') = raw, 0) AS ok,
       CASE WHEN strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ', raw, '+0 seconds') = raw
            THEN datetime(raw) END AS ts
FROM stamps;
--- hint
`datetime()` is generous: it reads almost any shape, rolls impossible dates over, and without a modifier lets hour 24 through. Test with a round trip instead: write the moment back in the exact format, and compare with the text.
--- hint
`strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ', raw, '+0 seconds') = raw`. The `'+0 seconds'` forces the date arithmetic. For a NULL `raw` the comparison is NULL, so wrap it in `COALESCE(…, 0)`.
--- check query | Only the three real, exact moments pass
SELECT id, ok, ts FROM stamp_check ORDER BY id
=> [[1, 1, "2026-03-01 10:00:00"], [2, 0, null], [3, 1, "2028-02-29 10:00:00"], [4, 0, null], [5, 0, null], [6, 0, null], [7, 0, null], [8, 1, "2026-03-01 23:59:59"], [9, 0, null]]
--- check query | 29 February passes in 2028 and fails in 2026
SELECT id, ok FROM stamp_check WHERE id IN (2, 3) ORDER BY id
=> [[2, 0], [3, 1]]
--- check query | Hour 24 and a NULL both fail, with ok = 0, not NULL
SELECT id, ok, ts FROM stamp_check WHERE id IN (4, 9) ORDER BY id
=> [[4, 0, null], [9, 0, null]]

+++ practice | The CAST that read "n/a" as zero
--- schema

--- task
This view is meant to keep only the voltages that arrived as JSON numbers, but it lets `"n/a"`, `"12abc"` and JSON `true` through as 0.0, 12.0 and 1.0:

```sql
CREATE VIEW good_volts AS
SELECT line_no, CAST(v_raw AS REAL) AS volts
FROM stg_volt
WHERE CAST(v_raw AS REAL) IS NOT NULL;
```

The table is `stg_volt (line_no, v_raw, v_type)`, where `v_type` is the JSON type the value arrived as. Fix `good_volts`, keeping its name and columns, so it keeps exactly the rows whose value was a JSON number.
--- starter
CREATE VIEW good_volts AS
SELECT line_no, CAST(v_raw AS REAL) AS volts
FROM stg_volt
WHERE CAST(v_raw AS REAL) IS NOT NULL;
--- solution
CREATE VIEW good_volts AS
SELECT line_no, CAST(v_raw AS REAL) AS volts
FROM stg_volt
WHERE v_type IN ('integer', 'real');
--- hint
`CAST` never returns NULL for text: it takes whatever number it finds at the start and makes the rest zero. So `CAST(…) IS NOT NULL` is true for every row.
--- hint
Decide on what the packet sent, not on what `CAST` makes of it: keep the rows whose `v_type` is `'integer'` or `'real'`.

+++ practice | A rerun that forgot the triage
--- schema
CREATE TABLE stg (batch_id INTEGER, line_no INTEGER, body TEXT, reason TEXT);
INSERT INTO stg VALUES (3, 1, 'x', 'malformed_json'), (3, 2, '{}', 'missing_field'), (3, 3, '{"v":1}', NULL);
CREATE TABLE quarantine (
  batch_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  line_no  INTEGER NOT NULL,
  reason   TEXT NOT NULL,
  body     TEXT,
  resolved INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  PRIMARY KEY (batch_id, line_no)
);
CREATE TABLE requeue (request_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, batch_id INTEGER NOT NULL);
--- task
Rejected rows of `stg (batch_id, line_no, body, reason)` are copied into `quarantine` by a trigger on `requeue`, one request per run. People set `resolved = 1` on rows they have looked at. The current trigger deletes the batch's quarantine rows and inserts them again, so every rerun wipes the `resolved` flags:

```sql
CREATE TRIGGER quarantine_batch AFTER INSERT ON requeue
BEGIN
  DELETE FROM quarantine WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id;
  INSERT INTO quarantine (batch_id, line_no, reason, body)
  SELECT batch_id, line_no, reason, body FROM stg
  WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id AND reason IS NOT NULL;
END;
```

Rewrite `quarantine_batch` so a rerun refreshes `reason` and `body`, keeps `resolved`, and still removes the quarantine rows of lines that are no longer rejected. The script then runs batch 3 once with `INSERT INTO requeue (batch_id) VALUES (3);`.
--- starter
CREATE TRIGGER quarantine_batch AFTER INSERT ON requeue
BEGIN
  DELETE FROM quarantine WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id;
  INSERT INTO quarantine (batch_id, line_no, reason, body)
  SELECT batch_id, line_no, reason, body FROM stg
  WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id AND reason IS NOT NULL;
END;

INSERT INTO requeue (batch_id) VALUES (3);
--- solution
CREATE TRIGGER quarantine_batch AFTER INSERT ON requeue
BEGIN
  DELETE FROM quarantine
  WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id
    AND line_no NOT IN (SELECT line_no FROM stg
                        WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id AND reason IS NOT NULL);
  INSERT INTO quarantine (batch_id, line_no, reason, body)
  SELECT batch_id, line_no, reason, body FROM stg
  WHERE batch_id = NEW.batch_id AND reason IS NOT NULL
  ON CONFLICT (batch_id, line_no) DO UPDATE SET
    reason = excluded.reason,
    body   = excluded.body;
END;

INSERT INTO requeue (batch_id) VALUES (3);
--- hint
Delete only what should go: the batch's quarantine rows whose line is not among its rejected lines any more. Every other row stays, flag and all.
--- hint
Turn the insert into an upsert: `… ON CONFLICT (batch_id, line_no) DO UPDATE SET reason = excluded.reason, body = excluded.body`. Leaving `resolved` out of the `SET` is what keeps it.
--- check query | The first run quarantines two lines
SELECT line_no, reason, resolved FROM quarantine ORDER BY line_no
=> [[1, "malformed_json", 0], [2, "missing_field", 0]]
--- check query | A rerun keeps the flag someone set
UPDATE quarantine SET resolved = 1 WHERE line_no = 1;
INSERT INTO requeue (batch_id) VALUES (3);
SELECT line_no, resolved FROM quarantine ORDER BY line_no
=> [[1, 1], [2, 0]]
--- check query | A line fixed upstream leaves quarantine, a changed reason is refreshed
UPDATE stg SET reason = NULL WHERE line_no = 2;
UPDATE stg SET reason = 'bad_timestamp' WHERE line_no = 1;
INSERT INTO requeue (batch_id) VALUES (3);
SELECT line_no, reason, resolved FROM quarantine ORDER BY line_no
=> [[1, "bad_timestamp", 1]]

=== cap-data-04 | Data system 4: the star schema
--- teach
Last milestone split staging into clean rows and quarantined ones. The clean rows are still in the shape they arrived in: codes, text times, one row per packet, duplicates and all. This milestone builds the shape the questions need, a **star schema**, and the load step that fills it.

### Why a second shape

The operational schema is normalised: perfect for editing, and slow and awkward for questions. "Average battery voltage per satellite per ops shift" would join readings to sensors to satellites, and cut the times into shifts, in every report, and every report would do it slightly differently.

A **dimensional model** splits the world into two kinds of table:

- A **fact table** holds the measurements: one row per event, with a few numbers and keys. It is long, and it grows forever.
- **Dimension tables** hold the context of a fact: who, what, when, where. They are short, wide and descriptive, and they rarely change.

Drawn out, the fact table sits in the middle with a dimension at the end of each key, like the points of a [[star|star-shape]]. Every question takes the same form: filter and group by dimension columns, and add up fact columns.

| table | one row is | rows here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fact_reading` | one reading of one sensor at one moment | 5,379 |
| `dim_sensor` | a sensor, with its satellite, type, label and unit | 23 |
| `dim_satellite` | a satellite, with its code, name and status | 6 |
| `dim_time` | one hour of the calendar | 48 |
| `dim_station` | a ground station (for milestone 6) | 4 |

### The grain

The first decision in any fact table is its **grain**: exactly what one row means. Here it is *one reading of one sensor at one moment*. Every other choice follows from it, and the table enforces it with `UNIQUE (sensor_key, ts)`. A second row for the same sensor and moment would be counted twice by every `COUNT` and `SUM` in every report, and nothing downstream could tell.

### Surrogate keys

A dimension row gets a **surrogate key**: a plain integer the warehouse assigns, like `sensor_key`, which means nothing outside the warehouse. The operational identifier, the **natural key** (`sensor_id`), is kept as a `UNIQUE` column, and the load uses it to find the surrogate.

Why not join facts to `sensor_id` directly? Because the warehouse must not depend on how another system numbers things. The operational team may renumber sensors, a second source may bring its own ids, and a later version of the warehouse may keep [[several versions of one sensor|scd]], each with its own key. Surrogate keys are also small and fast to join. The load assigns them in order of the natural key, so the same input always gives the same keys.

### A dimension may repeat itself

`dim_sensor` copies the satellite's code and the type's label and unit into every sensor row. In milestone 1 that was the update anomaly. Here it is deliberate: reports join the fact table to one dimension instead of three. It is safe because nobody edits a dimension by hand. The load rebuilds it from the operational tables on every run, with an upsert, so a change there reaches every copy.

`dim_station` does the same for ground stations, and adds a **derived attribute**, `hemisphere`: `'N'` when the latitude is 0 or more, `'S'` otherwise. Working it out once, in the dimension, beats working it out in every report.

### The calendar

`dim_time` has one row per hour. Its key is the hour written as a number, `YYYYMMDDHH`: `2026030114` is 14:00 on 1 March. An integer key sorts in time order, joins fast, and can be read by a person. The row carries what reports group by: `hour_start`, `day`, `hour`, `weekday` (0 is Sunday, from `strftime('%w', …)`) and `shift`, the operations shift: `'A'` from 00:00, `'B'` from 08:00, `'C'` from 16:00.

The calendar must have **no holes**. An hour in which no sensor reported still gets a row, because "which hours were empty?" is a question the reports will ask in milestone 8, and a missing row cannot be counted. So the load does not add the hours that have readings. It adds every hour from the earliest hour it knows, in the calendar or in this batch, to the latest.

A recursive CTE counts through the hours. Inside a trigger a statement cannot start with `WITH`, so the CTE goes inside a subquery in the `FROM`:

```sql fragment
INSERT OR IGNORE INTO some_calendar (...)
SELECT ... FROM (
  WITH RECURSIVE h (t) AS (
    SELECT <first hour>
    UNION ALL
    SELECT datetime(t, '+1 hour') FROM h WHERE t < <last hour>
  )
  SELECT t FROM h
);
```

`INSERT OR IGNORE` skips the hours that already exist, so running it again is harmless. `strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:00:00', ts)` rounds a moment down to its hour.

### Duplicates inside a batch

A ground station sometimes sends the same reading twice in one batch. Batch 1 repeats four of ORB-1's readings from 05:00 at its end, and batch 2 sends ORB-3's CPU temperature for 18:20 three times, with three different values. The rule: **for one sensor and moment, the batch's last line wins**, because a sender that repeats itself is correcting itself.

`DISTINCT` cannot do this: two copies with different values are distinct, so both stay. The tool is the "keep the latest row" pattern from the expert course. Number the copies of each (batch, sensor, moment) from the last line down, and keep number 1:

```sql fragment
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY batch_id, sensor_id, ts ORDER BY line_no DESC) AS copy_rank
... WHERE copy_rank = 1
```

The view `v_stg_accepted` does this for the clean rows of every batch, and also turns each `sensor_id` into its `sensor_key` and each `ts` into its `time_key`. The load step and, later, the rollups read from it.

### The load step

```text
load(batch b):
  1. upsert dim_satellite, dim_sensor, dim_station from the operational tables
  2. add every missing hour to dim_time, from the earliest to the latest known
  3. insert b's accepted rows into fact_reading; a reading already there stays
  4. log: rows_in = b's clean staged rows, rows_out = facts from batch b
```

The order matters. The fact table's foreign keys point at the dimensions, so the dimensions and the calendar must be complete before the facts arrive. Step 3 uses `ON CONFLICT (sensor_key, ts) DO NOTHING` for now: the first version of a reading is kept. Milestone 5 will ask whether that is right.

One piece of SQLite syntax needs care. In `INSERT INTO t SELECT … FROM a JOIN b ON … ON CONFLICT …`, SQLite cannot tell whether the second `ON` belongs to the join. A `WHERE` clause before `ON CONFLICT` removes the doubt, even `WHERE true`.

### Why the load is correct

After step 3, `fact_reading` holds exactly one row for every (sensor, moment) that appears in a clean row of any loaded batch. There is at most one, because `UNIQUE (sensor_key, ts)` refuses a second. There is at least one, because each accepted row is either inserted or, if its key is already there, skipped because it is already there. Rerunning a batch finds all its keys present and changes nothing: the step is idempotent.

### What it costs

The window numbers the copies with a sort by (batch, sensor, moment): O(n log n) for n staged rows. Each fact insert checks the unique index: O(log F) for F facts, so a batch of n rows costs O(n log F). The dimension upserts touch a few dozen rows, and the calendar adds at most one row per hour of new data.

### Where this is used

This is the design from [[Ralph Kimball's books|kimball]], and it is still how most analytics databases and business intelligence tools are organised. Spacecraft operations centres keep their telemetry archives the same way: a huge table of readings keyed by parameter and time, and small tables that describe each parameter.

**Watch out:** the calendar has to cover the gap between batches, not just the hours of this batch. If batch 5 arrives after a day with no data, building hours only from batch 5's own readings leaves a day-long hole. Always fill from the earliest known hour to the latest.

::: context star-shape Why it is called a star
Draw the fact table as a box in the middle and each dimension as a box around it, with a line for each key, and the picture looks like a star. When dimensions have dimensions of their own, for example `dim_sensor` pointing at a separate `dim_sensor_type` table, the picture branches like a snowflake, and that design is called a snowflake schema. This warehouse copies the type's label and unit into `dim_sensor` instead, which keeps it a star and saves a join in every report.
:::

::: context scd Keeping the history of a dimension
A satellite's status changes: active, safe mode, active again. If the dimension simply overwrites the status, every old reading now looks as if it was taken in the current status. That is called a type 1 dimension, and it is what this warehouse does. A type 2 dimension instead adds a new row, with a new surrogate key, each time an attribute changes, and each fact points at the version that was true when it happened. Surrogate keys are what make that possible. Milestone 11 solves the same problem a different way, with a status history table.
:::

::: context kimball Two ways to organise a warehouse
Ralph Kimball's approach, from the 1990s, builds star schemas around business processes: one fact table per process, sharing dimensions like time. Bill Inmon's approach first builds one fully normalised company-wide store and derives stars from it. Most real warehouses mix the two. This project has both layers in miniature: a normalised operational schema, and stars loaded from it. The second fact table in milestone 6, for ground station passes, will share the time and satellite dimensions with this one.
:::
--- task
The tables `dim_satellite`, `dim_sensor`, `dim_station`, `dim_time` and `fact_reading` are in the starter, and `'load'` has been added to the steps of a run.

1. Give `fact_reading` the constraint `UNIQUE (sensor_key, ts)`.
2. Replace the stub view `v_stg_accepted` with a view of the columns `batch_id`, `line_no`, `sensor_key`, `time_key`, `ts`, `value`: the clean rows of `stg_reading` (no `reject_reason`), keeping only the one with the highest `line_no` for each (`batch_id`, `sensor_id`, `ts`), with `sensor_key` from `dim_sensor` and `time_key = CAST(strftime('%Y%m%d%H', ts) AS INTEGER)`.
3. Replace the stub trigger `etl_load` (after a row is inserted into `etl_step` whose `step` is `'load'`) with one that, in this order:
   - upserts every satellite into `dim_satellite` (`sat_id`, `sat_code` from `code`, `sat_name` from `name`, `status`), in order of `sat_id`, updating the other columns on a conflict on `sat_id`;
   - upserts every sensor into `dim_sensor` (`sensor_id`, the satellite's `sat_key` and `sat_code`, `type_code`, `type_label` from the type's `label`, `unit`), in order of `sensor_id`, updating `sat_key`, `sat_code`, `type_label` and `unit` on a conflict on `sensor_id`;
   - upserts every ground station into `dim_station` (`station_id`, `station_code`, `station_name`, `hemisphere` = `'N'` when `latitude >= 0`, else `'S'`), in order of `station_id`, updating the other columns on a conflict on `station_id`;
   - inserts, ignoring the ones that exist, one `dim_time` row for every hour from the earliest to the latest of: the hours already in `dim_time`, and the hours of the batch's clean rows. The columns are `time_key` (`YYYYMMDDHH` as an integer), `hour_start` (`'YYYY-MM-DD HH:00:00'`), `day`, `hour` (an integer), `weekday` (an integer from `strftime('%w', …)`) and `shift` (`'A'` before 08:00, `'B'` before 16:00, else `'C'`);
   - inserts the batch's rows of `v_stg_accepted` into `fact_reading`, doing nothing on a conflict on `(sensor_key, ts)`;
   - sets the step row's `rows_in` to the batch's clean staged rows and `rows_out` to the facts whose `batch_id` is the batch.
4. The test: insert into `expect_count` the rows `('facts', 'ORB-1', 1144)`, `('facts', 'ORB-2', 1137)`, `('facts', 'ORB-3', 1104)`, `('facts', 'ORB-4', 1148)`, `('facts', 'ORB-5', 846)`, `('dims', 'dim_satellite', 6)`, `('dims', 'dim_sensor', 23)`, `('dims', 'dim_station', 4)`, `('dims', 'dim_time', 48)`. Replace the stub `test_star` with a view of the columns `test`, `item`, `expected`, `actual` that returns the rows where these counts and the star disagree: facts per satellite code, and the row count of each dimension.
--- starter
-- =====================================================================
--  ORBIT fleet telemetry warehouse
--
--  One script builds the whole database from an empty file that holds
--  only the landing zone (landing_packet). The layers, in the order the
--  data flows through them:
--
--    1. operational schema   the fleet, as the operations team keeps it
--    2. pipeline control     runs and steps, one trigger per step
--    3. staging              every landed packet, parsed, not trusted
--    4. quarantine           rejected packets, each with one reason
--    5. star schema          dimensions and the fact table
--    6. rollups              hourly and daily aggregates
--    7. trend reports        window functions over the facts
--    8. gaps and islands     outages, empty hours, low-battery streaks
--    9. data quality         checks that must return zero rows
--   10. report suite         what operations reads every morning
--
--  Conventions: times are UTC text 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'; every step can
--  be rerun for the same batch without changing the result.
-- =====================================================================

PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------
-- 1. Operational schema: the fleet as the operations team keeps it.
--    Normalised: each fact about the fleet is stored exactly once, and
--    the constraints refuse any row that could not be true.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE TABLE satellite (
  sat_id       INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  code         TEXT    NOT NULL UNIQUE CHECK (code GLOB 'ORB-[0-9]*'),
  name         TEXT    NOT NULL,
  launched_on  TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (launched_on IS date(launched_on)),
  status       TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active'
                       CHECK (status IN ('active', 'safe_mode', 'retired')),
  status_since TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (status_since >= launched_on)
);

CREATE TABLE sensor_type (
  type_code  TEXT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY CHECK (type_code = lower(type_code)),
  label      TEXT NOT NULL,
  unit       TEXT NOT NULL,
  min_valid  REAL NOT NULL,
  max_valid  REAL NOT NULL,
  CHECK (min_valid < max_valid)
);

CREATE TABLE sensor (
  sensor_id  INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  sat_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES satellite (sat_id),
  type_code  TEXT    NOT NULL REFERENCES sensor_type (type_code),
  UNIQUE (sat_id, type_code)
);

CREATE TABLE ground_station (
  station_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  code       TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE CHECK (length(code) = 3 AND code = upper(code)),
  name       TEXT NOT NULL,
  latitude   REAL NOT NULL CHECK (latitude BETWEEN -90 AND 90),
  longitude  REAL NOT NULL CHECK (longitude BETWEEN -180 AND 180)
);

-- A planned contact: the satellite is above the station's horizon from
-- aos (acquisition of signal) until los (loss of signal).
CREATE TABLE contact_pass (
  pass_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  sat_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES satellite (sat_id),
  station_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES ground_station (station_id),
  aos        TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (aos IS datetime(aos, '+0 seconds')),
  los        TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (los IS datetime(los, '+0 seconds')),
  CHECK (los > aos),
  UNIQUE (sat_id, aos)
);
